IMPORTANT
IMPORTANT NOTICE TO INVESTORS:
FULLY ELECTRONIC APPLICATION PROCESS
We have adopted a fully electronic application process for the Hong Kong Public
Offering. We will not provide printed copies of this prospectus to the public in relation to the
Hong Kong Public Offering.
This prospectus is available at the website of the Stock Exchange at www.hkexnews.hk
under the “HKEXnews > New Listings > New Listing Information” section, and our website
at zhihuimining.com. If you require a printed copy of this prospectus, you may download and
print from the website addresses above.
To apply for the Hong Kong Offer Shares, you may:
(1) apply online through the White Form eIPO service at www.eipo.com.hk; or
(2) apply through the HKSCC EIPO channel to electronically cause HKSCC Nominees to apply
on your behalf, including by instructing your broker or custodian who is a HKSCC
Participant to submit electronic application instruction on your behalf through HKSCC’s FINI
system in accordance with your instruction.
We will not provide any physical channels to accept any application for the Hong Kong Offer
Shares by the public. The contents of the electronic version of this prospectus are identical to the
printed prospectus as registered with the Registrar of Companies in Hong Kong pursuant to Section
342C of the Companies (Winding Up and Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance (Chapter 32 of the
Laws of Hong Kong).
If you are an intermediary, broker or agent, please remind your customers, clients or
principals, as applicable, that this prospectus is available online at the website addresses above.
See “How to Apply for Hong Kong Offer Shares” in this prospectus for further details on the
procedures through which you can apply for the Hong Kong Offer Shares electronically.

SUMMARY
This summary aims to give you an overview of the information contained in this prospectus.
As this is a summary, it does not contain all the information that may be important to you. You
should read the entire prospectus before you decide to invest in the Offer Shares. There are risks
associated with any investment. Some of the particular risks in investing in the Offer Shares are
set out in “Risk Factors” in this prospectus. You should read that section carefully before you
decide to invest in the Offer Shares.
OVERVIEW
We are a mining company focusing our business on zinc, lead and copper exploration, mining,
production and sales of concentrates based in Xizang, China. According to SMM, in terms of the
average annual production volume in Xizang in 2024, we ranked fifth for zinc concentrates, fourth for
lead concentrates and fifth for copper concentrates. In 2024, we accounted for 11.1% of the total zinc
concentrates production, 4.2% of the total lead concentrates production and 0.1% of the total copper
concentrate production in Xizang, respectively. The production of lead concentrates and copper
concentrates in Xizang are dominated by leading companies. In 2024, the top two companies, both
locally based in Xizang, accounted for 36.1% and 31.6% of total market share of lead concentrates
production; and the top two companies, both locally based in Xizang, accounted for 44.2% and 42.3%
of total market share of copper concentrates production in Xizang.
Our mining operations are located in Rongdoi Township, Jiali County, Nagqu, Xizang. Our
Mengya’a Mine comprises an open-pit mine which has been in commercial operation since 2007, and
an underground mine, which has commenced commercial operation since the second quarter of 2025.
Our mining operations are located within the nationally designated Jinda Integrated ExplorationArea
at an altitude between 5,000.0 m asl and 5,300.0 m asl where rich mineral resources have been found.
We hold exploration rights over an area of approximately 58.5 sq.km and mining rights over an area
of approximately 4.5 sq.km., respectively.
As a mining company in Xizang, we believe we need to consistently adopt a localised business
approach, taking into account the unique geography and Xizang’s specific policies to ensure our
business can adapt to the local conditions and lead to ongoing business sustainability and success.As
at 31 July 2025, our open-pit mine contained total ore reserves of 1,438.0 kt at average grades of
4.90% Zn, 0.69% Pb, 0.10% Cu and 10.09 g/t Ag; and our underground mine contained total ore
reserves of 10,623.0 kt at average grades of 4.14% Zn, 2.99% Pb, 0.21% Cu and 35.00 g/t Ag. Our
Mengya’a Mine can, in aggregate, supply 400.0 kt of ores annually for concentrate production at our
processing plant.
We have a business operation chain that encompasses exploration, mining, production and sales
of concentrates. Our main products include zinc, lead and copper concentrates. Our revenue is
generated from sales of these concentrates to our customers in China. Our customers include
nonferrous metal traders who conduct onward sales of concentrates to end users of concentrates; and
refineries which further process our concentrates depending on their customers’ needs. Specifically,
nonferrous metal traders purchase our concentrates and conduct onward sales to refineries to generate
profits. The downstream refinery customers cover various regions in China, and most of them are
listed companies and/or state-owned enterprises. Refineries refine zinc, lead and copper concentrates
into metal ingots.

200.0 kt alone assuming each of the open-pit mine and underground mine contributes to half of the
permitted annual mining capacity of 400.0 kt and our underground mine had a remaining LOM of 31.0
years.

=== PAGE 15 ===
SUMMARY
• Exploration: Our extensive exploration programmes from 2004 to 2021 allowed us to
identify mineralised deposits within our exploration licensed area through mapping,
sampling, trenching and drilling, with a focus on refining resource estimates. In late 2024,
we conducted an infill and validation programme to refine resource classifications and
verify exploration data. During the Track Record Period, we possessed patents of
exploration that we believe would provide us a competitive advantage. See “Business —
Exploration” in this prospectus for details. During the Track Record Period, while we are
responsible for planning, formulating implementation plans and overseeing quality control
for exploration and mining activities, all exploration and mining operations are entirely
outsourced to subcontractors. See “Business — Mining — Exploration and Mining
Subcontracting Arrangement” in this prospectus for details.
• Mining: During the Track Record Period, we have engaged subcontractors to undertake
demolition, drilling, blasting and excavation works. In recent years, we have also
diversified our ore resources through external procurement for consistent product quality
and enhanced operational efficiency. See “Business — Mining — Management System of
Exploration and Mining Activities” and “ Business — Mining — Management Discussion
on Ore Procurement” in this prospectus for details.
• Production: Our Mengya’a Beneficiation Plant processes ores into zinc, lead and copper
concentrates by blending, crushing, grinding, flotation and product dewatering. We
constructed a pre-concentration plant at the open-pit site, using intelligent sorting to
process mineralised waste which have been obtained during our exploration and project
development processes. For the years ended 31 December 2022, 2023, 2024 and the seven
months ended 31 July 2025, the ore processing volume was approximately 354.0 kt, 374.2
kt, 321.8 kt and 204.6 kt, respectively. See “Business — Production” in this prospectus for
details.
• Sale of concentrates: Our main products are zinc concentrates, lead concentrates and
copper concentrates. All of our revenue was generated from sale of concentrates. For the
years ended 31 December 2022, 2023, 2024 and the seven months ended 31 July 2025,
revenue from our sales of concentrates were approximately RMB482.4 million, RMB546.1
million, RMB301.4 million and RMB256.6 million, respectively. Revenue from
concentrate sales is recognised upon transfer of control of products to customers, following
inspection and testing of the products. A transportation service provider manages delivery
of concentrates from our processing plant to Lhasa.

COMPETITION
The competitive landscape for zinc, lead and copper concentrates in China is characterised by
a combination of domestic production dynamics, global supply chain challenges and fluctuating
demand. The future development for the zinc, lead and copper concentrates will depend on the market
players’ ability to address these challenges while capitalising on emerging opportunities. In Xizang,
the annual lead concentrate production was approximately 88.2 kt in 2024; the annual zinc concentrate
production was approximately 111.3 kt in 2024; and the annual copper concentrate production was
approximately 376.4 kt in 2024, respectively.
See “Business — Competition” in this prospectus for details.

COMPETITIVE STRENGTHS
We believe we possess the following competitive strengths:
• we enjoy a distinct advantage in Xizang for our sufficient and high-calibre mineral
resources given the region’s geographical characteristics;
• our business operations have local community engagement and close local interactions;
• the longevity of expanded tailings storage capacity is well-positioned to support our mining
operations and demonstrates our commitment to, and resilience in sustainable mining
activities;
• we possess technological expertise and a dedicated and stable talent pool to ensure our
continued success; and
• a dependable and experienced management team and an inclusive group culture.
See “Business — Competitive Strengths” in this prospectus for details.

• upgrading ore processing and concentrate production capability and capacity for our
sustainable growth; and
• investment in and acquisition of mining assets.

Revenue from sales of concentrates is generally influenced by the quantity of the concentrates

influenced by the utilisation of our processing plant, which might be influenced by the optimisation
plan of the plant, among other factors. Our revenue for the year ended 31 December 2024 significantly
decreased primarily due to (i) shortened production period (we customarily resume operations in
April; however, adverse weather conditions delayed the 2024 resumption until May) and (ii) the
sequential upgrade of two production lines as result of which our processing plant was in partial
operation from May to October 2024. Our revenue for the seven months ended 31 July 2025
significantly increased from that for the seven months ended 31 July 2024 primarily due to key factors
including (i) normal production period (we resumed operations in April 2025 with no exceptional
delay), (ii) full utilisation of two production lines upon the completion of our processing plant
upgrade since October 2024, and (iii) an increase in concentrate output due to an increase in ore
grades of mined ores and externally procured ores where higher-grade ores generally yield higher
outputs and generate more revenue.

=== PAGE 23 ===
SUMMARY
The Directors are of the view that the decrease in our revenue in 2024 was temporary and was
not expected to have any material adverse effect on our Group’s operations and business prospects in
the foreseeable future. The decrease was caused by the rotational update to production lines in 2024,
which was a natural operational requirement out of the actual operational development at that time
and based on our Group’s technology innovation strategy. It has a long-term financial benefit to our
Group as it significantly increases our Group’s comprehensive utilisation capability and it had already
delivered positive financial contributions during in the year of 2024. The short-term dip in financial
performance, while still producing an acceptable absolute profit of over RMB55.0 million,
represented a prudent trade-off for attaining higher profit levels in future years. According to the
audited financial statements of the stub period ended at 31 July 2025, our Group had resumed its
normal production and is expected to achieve the profit level in 2025 similar to the profit level in 2022
and 2023.

2025. The increase in net profit and the increase in our revenue and gross profit from 2022 to 2023
was primarily attributable to the increase in revenue from sales of lead concentrates and copper
concentrates driven by the increases in both sales volume and the average selling price of such
concentrates in 2023. The decrease in net profit and the decrease in our revenue and gross profit from
2023 to 2024 was primarily attributable to production line upgrades and weather-induced delays in
2024. The increase in net profit and the increase in our revenue and gross profit from seven months
ended 31 July 2024 to seven months ended 31 July 2025 was mainly driven by an increase in the sales
volume across all of our concentrates in 2025. See detailed reasons for the change in revenue and
gross profit in respective year/period in “Summary of Financial Information” of this prospectus.

KEY RISK FACTORS
We believe the following are some of the major key risks that may have an impact on our
business and financial performance:
• fluctuations in the market price of zinc, lead and copper concentrates could materially and
adversely affect our profitability and cash flow;
• our existing mining operations have a finite life;
• as we continue the exploration and mining process, the ore grade of our Mengya’a Mine
is expected to decrease over time;
• business operation in Xizang presents unique challenges, particularly due to the high
altitude which can have serious implications for the health and safety of our employees;
• our operations are subject to risks relating to occupational hazards and production safety;
• our business is subject to climate and weather conditions of Xizang Plateau; and
• we face certain risks and uncertainties beyond our control from natural disasters that may
negatively impact our mining operations.
See “Risk Factors” in this prospectus for details.

SUMMARY
ENVIRONMENTAL REHABILITATION
According to the relevant PRC laws and regulations, we are required to be responsible for site
closure and land rehabilitation in relation to mining activities and submit a land rehabilitation plan
to the Ministry of Natural Resources of the PRC (中華人民共和國自然資源部) or the local land and
resources branch for review when renewing the mining licences. The purpose of land rehabilitation
is to rehabilitate the land damaged by the mining operations in order to control water and soil loss
and protect the ecological environment. We have a land rehabilitation plan, and we recognise
provision for environmental rehabilitation and restoration costs for mines pursuant to the regulations
of Nagqu in which our mining operations are located. The amount of the provision is estimated based
on the life of mining tenement, timing of mine closure and cost of such rehabilitation, and such
estimation basis will be updated annually. For the years ended 31 December 2022, 2023, 2024 and the
seven months ended 31 July 2025, provisions made for environmental rehabilitation and restoration
costs for mines were approximately RMB9.8 million, RMB9.3 million, RMB9.7 million and RMB7.3
million, respectively. See “Business — Environment, Social and Governance — Environmental
Protection — Environmental rehabilitation” and “Financial Information — Selected Balance Sheet
Items — Provision” in this prospectus for the details of our land rehabilitation plan and the movement
of provision made for site closure and land rehabilitation purposes during the Track Record Period.
We also have our own ESG policies with respect of environmental rehabilitation. Our ESG policies
mainly include environmental protection policies, mine land reclamation plan 《( 礦山地質環境保護與
土地復墾方案》), human resources policies, occupational health and safety policies, operation
management policies and business ethics policies and rules, which provide important guidance for our
sustainability practices, allow us to oversee the implementation of ESG measures and demonstrate our
commitment to business integrity, talent development, environmental protection and community
development.
REGULATORY COMPLIANCE
During the Track Record Period and up to the Latest Practicable Date, we were in full
compliance with the relevant PRC laws and regulations. In respect of our mining and exploration
licences, we had not been penalised by any government authorities for any issues. To the best of our
Directors’knowledge, we currently do not expect to encounter any difficulty in renewing them when
they expire, if applicable, and no unexpected or adverse changes have occurred since the date of their
respective issuance.
As advised by our PRC Legal Advisers, during the Track Record Period and up to the Latest
Practicable Date, we had complied in all material aspects with the applicable PRC laws and
regulations relating to environmental protection; we had not received any notice or warning, nor had
we been subject to any investigation or suffered any fines or penalties that would have a material
adverse effect on our production and operations as a result of any breach of the relevant PRC
environmental laws and regulations.

GLOSSARY OF TECHNICAL TERMS
This glossary contains definitions of certain terms used in this prospectus in connection with our
Company and our business. Some of these may not correspond to standard industry definitions.
“5G” the latest advancement in cellular network technology. It
offers significant improvements over 4G in terms of speed,
latency, and capacity, enabling new possibilities for mobile
devices, IoT, and various industries
“μm” micrometres, equal to one millionth of a metre
“-200 mesh” a sieve or filter with openings that allow particles smaller
than approximately 74 microns in size to pass through
“Ag” silver
“alloy” mixture of two or more elements in which the primary
component is a metal
“asl” above sea level
“assay sample” a representative portion of a mineral deposit or ore that is
collected and analysed to determine its composition and
quality
“ball mill” type of grinder used to grind or blend materials into fine
powder
“Bangonghu-Nujiang Suture” significant geological feature located in central Xizang,
separating the Qiangtang terrane to the north from the Lhasa
terrane to the south
“beneficiation” process involving the removal of gangue minerals from ore to
produce a higher-grade product
“blending ratio” proportion of different types of ores mixed together to
achieve a desired grade or quality for processing
“bulk density” a physical property of mineral components, defined by the
weight of an object or material divided by its volume,
including the volume of its pore spaces
“CAGR” compound annual growth rate
“carboniferous” time period 359 to 299 million years ago
“channel sample” sample collected by cutting a continuous groove or channel
into the rock face using tools such as chisels, saws, or drills.
The groove is typically uniform in width and depth to ensure
consistency

GLOSSARY OF TECHNICAL TERMS
“cm” centimetres
“comprehensive utilisation” refers to the scientific and rational methods used to blend ore
resources that might be difficult to utilise directly due to their
low-grade with high-grade ore. Comprehensive utilisation
optimises the overall quality of the ore materials, thereby
improving the efficiency and economic benefits during the
beneficiation processes
“compressive” the capacity of a material or structure to withstand loads
tending to reduce size, measured by plotting
“concentrate” concentrates are produced by separating zinc-, lead- and
copper- bearing minerals from other minerals and impurities
found in the ore. The concentration process often involves
crushing, grinding, and various separation techniques such as
flotation, gravity separation, or leaching. Our lead and copper
concentrates contain inseparable coexistent minerals
(伴生金屬) such as silver
“cone crusher” a type of crushing equipment to efficiently crush hard and
abrasive materials into smaller, manageable sizes
“copper-lead recovery” extraction and separation of copper and lead from ores or
waste materials like slag
“crusher” a machine designed to reduce the size of large rocks or other
materials into smaller, more manageable pieces
“crushing” process of breaking down large ore bodies into smaller,
manageable sizes to facilitate subsequent processing stages
like grinding and separation
“Cu” copper
“cut-off grade” minimum concentration of a valuable mineral or metal in ore
that makes it economically viable to extract and process
“cyclone” a device used in mineral processing and other industries to
classify and separate particles based on size and density
“cyclone feed slurry pump” type of pump specifically designed to feed slurries into
hydrocyclones for particle separation in mining and other
industrial applications
“deposit” naturally occurring concentration of minerals or metals that
can be economically extracted

“diamond twinned holes” diamond drill hole that is drilled very close to and in the same
orientation as an existing diamond drill hole
“double spiral classifier” type of equipment used in mineral processing to classify and
separate materials based on their size and density, featuring
two spiral blades that rotate to move materials through a tank
to allow for efficient classification and separation of fine and
coarse particles
“double-screw classifier” type of equipment used in mineral processing for the
classification and separation of materials based on size and
density, featuring two helical screws that rotate to move
materials through a tank or trough to allow for effective
classification of ore slurries
“drill hole” a hole drilled in the ground by a drill rig, usually for

allow sampling of rock material
“East Tethyan Orogenic Belt” a significant geological feature that formed as a result of the
tectonic processes associated with the closure of the Tethys
Ocean. This orogenic belt extends across several countries,
including parts of Turkey, Iran, and the Caucasus region. It is
characterised by complex geological formations, including
folded and faulted sedimentary rocks, metamorphic rocks,
and igneous intrusions
“electric vibrating feeder” type of vibrating feeder that uses electric power to generate
vibrations, which are then transmitted to a feeding trough or
tube
“EqPb grade” equivalent lead grade, which is a method used to express the

in terms of a single metal, typically lead
“exploration” activities undertaken to prove the location, volume and

“explosives depot” specialised facility designed for the safe storage of

“feed size” maximum size of material that can be fed into the crusher or

“filter press” a mechanical device used in various industries, including

such as grinding and flotation
“five fixed” principles of guidelines used to ensure effective lubrication management in
lubrication equipment maintenance, including “fixed point”, “fixed
quality”, “fixed time”, “fixed quantity” and “fixed person”
“flotation” process in exploration and project development for separating
valuable minerals i.e., high-grade ore from mineralised waste
by exploiting differences in their hydrophobicity
“flotation cells” components for the separation and concentration of valuable
minerals like copper, lead, and zinc, operating by introducing
air into a slurry of finely ground ore, causing hydrophobic
minerals to attach to air bubbles and rise to the surface,
forming a froth that is skimmed off as a concentrate
“flotation column” a device used in exploration and project development to
separate valuable minerals i.e., high-grade ore from
mineralised waste by feeding a slurry into the top and
introducing air bubbles at the bottom that would attach to
hydrophobic particles, which rise to form a froth rich in
valuable minerals
“flotation machine” a device used in exploration and project development to
separate valuable minerals i.e., high-grade ore from
mineralised waste by exploiting differences in their
hydrophobicity
“flotation test” test that assesses the efficiency of separating minerals based
on their surface properties

smelting, refining, and metal joining
“fold” a bend or flexure in a rock unit or series of rock units that has
been caused by crustal movements
“formation” a body of rock having a consistent set of characteristics
(lithology) that distinguish it from adjacent bodies of rock
“fresh ore” ore that has not been significantly altered by weathering or
oxidation processes

“scavenger flotation” stage in the flotation process that aims to recover any

“skarn” coarse-grained metamorphic rock formed through the

magmatic-hydrothermal fluids with carbonate rocks
“slope of regression” a fundamental aspect of linear regression analysis,
illustrating the relationship between the independent variable
(predictor) and the dependent variable (response). In the
context of Kriging estimates, the slope of the regression line
serves as an indicator of the quality of the estimation
“Songpan-Ganzi Terrane” significant geological region located in the northern part of

“sq.km.” square kilometres
“sq.m.” square metres
“stacking” arrangement of filter plates and frames to create chambers for

“stirring tank” a vessel used in various industrial processes to mix and blend
materials thoroughly
“stress regime” relative magnitudes of the principal stresses acting on the
Earth’s crust, which determine the type of faulting and
deformation that occurs
“strip ratio” critical metric in open-pit mining that measures the amount of
waste material (overburden) that must be removed to extract
a unit of ore

RISKS RELATING TO OUR BUSINESS AND INDUSTRY
Fluctuations in the market price of zinc, lead and copper concentrates could materially and
adversely affect our profitability and cash flow.
Our revenue is generated from the sales of zinc, lead and copper concentrates. Historically, while
the average price for zinc concentrates, lead concentrates and copper concentrates has increased in
value over time, such price may fluctuate and there can be no assurance that such price will not
continue to fluctuate in the future or that such prices will otherwise remain at sufficiently high levels
to support our profitability and cash flow. China’s zinc concentrate prices, influenced by refined zinc
prices and treatment charges, increased from RMB17,788.0 per tonne in 2018 to a sharp surge at
approximately RMB19,073.0 per tonne in 2022, followed by a decline to RMB15,322.0 per tonne in
2023 and rebounded to RMB19,020.0 per tonne in 2024. Lead concentrate prices decreased from
RMB17,462.0 per tonne in 2018 to RMB12,504.0 per tonne in 2020 due to oversupply but increased
thereafter because of supply shortages, reaching about RMB16,501.0 per tonne in 2024. Copper
concentrate prices steadily increased from RMB43,560.0 per tonne in 2018 to RMB69,146.0 per tonne
in 2024, driven by strong downstream demand and macroeconomic factors. See “Industry Overview”
in this prospectus for further details of the historical average selling price of zinc concentrates, lead
concentrates and copper concentrates from 2018 and 2024, and the projected trends for 2025 to 2028.
The average selling price for each of our zinc concentrates, lead concentrates and copper concentrates
has shown an upward trend, with that of zinc concentrates increasing from RMB14,989.0 per tonne
in 2022 to RMB17,510.0 per tonne in 2024, of lead concentrates rising from RMB14,895.0 per tonne
in 2022 to RMB19,496.0 per tonne in 2024, and of copper concentrates increasing from RMB59,859.0
per tonne in 2022 to RMB77,109.0 per tonne in 2024. For the seven months ended 31 July 2025, the
average selling price for each of our zinc concentrates, lead concentrates and copper concentrates was
RMB14,097.0 per tonne, RMB27,959.0 per tonne and RMB75,855.0 per tonne, respectively. See
“Business — Sales of Concentrates — Pricing” in this prospectus for further details of the average
annual selling price of our concentrates for the years ended 31 December 2022, 2023, 2024 and the
seven months ended 31 July 2025, respectively. Fluctuations of the price for zinc, lead and copper
concentrates may sometimes be difficult to predict, being dependent on numerous factors such as (i)
global macro-economic and political events and sentiments such as regional conflicts; (ii) supply and
demand for zinc concentrates and lead concentrates; (iii) interest rate and inflation rate expectations;
and (iv) actual and predicted behaviour of central banks in relation to mineral acquisition and
disposals. As our revenue was generated from our sales of lead, zinc and copper concentrates,
fluctuations in the market price of these products could affect our financial performance.

Our existing mining operations have a finite life.
Our existing mining operations have a finite life and will eventually close. According to the
Independent Technical Report, at the current designed production capacity, the LOMs of Pb14
open-pit mine and Pb12 underground mine are estimated at 8 and 31 years, respectively; the estimated
LOM of our Mengya’a Mine, on the combined basis, is 31 years. To sustain our concentrate
production and ensure long-term viability beyond the current defined mine lives, we must prioritise
reserve replacement strategies, including the conversion of Mineral Resources to Ore Reserves and
the discovery of new orebodies through exploration.
Key risks include insufficient capital allocation for exploration and feasibility studies,
uncertainties in exploration success, technical challenges such as geotechnical complexities or
declining ore grades, market volatility affecting commodity prices, and operational inefficiencies in
mine planning or infrastructure development. Failure to replenish reserves at a rate commensurate
with depletion could lead to reduced production volume of each of zinc, lead and copper concentrates,
diminishing revenue streams and cash flow post-LOM. This contraction could also lower the mineral
asset’s NPV, erode investor confidence, and limit access to capital for future projects. Prolonged
reserve shortfalls may further constrain strategic flexibility to adapt to market shifts or operational
disruptions. According to the Independent Technical Report, as at 31 July 2025, our Mengya’a Mine
is economically viable for another 31 years. Such economic analysis was carried out based on various
assumptions and factors. Therefore, in a hypothetical scenario where a decline in commodity prices,
combined with other technical factors, significantly impacts the economic viability of the mining
project, revenue could be reduced to the point where the project becomes uneconomic. In such a case,
the resulting financial strain may limit cash flow, reducing the ability to sustain operations and
ultimately leading to the failure to meet production targets. See relevant economic viability analysis
as presented in 14.3 of “Appendix III — Independent Technical Report” to this prospectus.
As we continue the exploration and mining process, the ore grade of our Mengya’a Mine is
expected to decrease over time.
The ore grade is a key determinant of the economic feasibility of mining operations.
Higher-grade ores generally yield higher outputs at lower processing costs, making them more
profitable. However, as high-grade deposits become exhausted, the ore grade may decrease over time.
Lower-grade ores require more intensive mining and processing efforts, leading to higher unit costs
and a substantial increase in overall operational costs. This shift may reduce our profit margins and
make it increasingly difficult to sustain operations. Furthermore, the exploration process itself is
inherently uncertain. While we may discover new mineral deposits, there is no guarantee that these
will possess the same quality as the existing reserves. If we encounter lower-grade ores during
exploration, it could necessitate a re-evaluation of our business model and operational strategies, such
as expediting the plan of comprehensive utilisation of mineralised waste. Such uncertainty further
complicates our ability to plan for the future, as we may face unexpected challenges that impact our
financial stability.

Our mining operations face risks related to occupational hazards and production safety due to
the high altitude of Xizang and the inherent risks brought by the use of explosives and other
dangerous articles.
Our mining operations are located at an altitude of over 5,000 m asl, which presents significant
challenges for our employees. One of the most serious risks associated with this high altitude is
altitude sickness, also known as acute mountain sickness (“AMS”). AMS occurs when people ascend
to high elevations, and their bodies struggle to acclimatise to the lower levels of oxygen in the air.
Symptoms can vary in severity and may include headaches, nausea, dizziness, fatigue, and shortness
of breath. In more severe cases, altitude sickness can lead to life-threatening conditions such as
high-altitude pulmonary edema or high-altitude cerebral edema, both of which require immediate
medical attention.
The nature of mining work often involves physical exertion, which increases the body’s need for
oxygen. This makes our employees more vulnerable to altitude sickness, especially if they are not
given adequate time to acclimatise. Some workers may begin to feel symptoms after only a short time
at high altitude, while others may take longer to adjust to the local conditions. Apart from altitude
sickness, workers in high-altitude regions such as Xizang face a higher risk of occupational diseases
compared to those in other areas, such as pulmonary edema and cardiovascular diseases. The
psychological effects of working in such extreme conditions can also contribute to the risks of altitude
sickness with increased levels of anxiety, depression and feelings of isolation. The physical symptoms
of altitude sickness combined with the demanding nature of mining work can exacerbate
psychological strain, making it difficult for workers to maintain emotional resilience.
Additionally, our mining operations involve the handling and storage of explosives and other
dangerous articles (such as explosives used in the mining process in which ores are extracted). There
may be risks of accidental detonation, fires or toxic exposure in the course of handling and storing
explosives during ore extraction. Accidents causing severe injuries or fatalities may happen to our
employees due to various reasons, such as the mishandling of dangerous articles in our mining
operations. There can be no assurance that such accidents will not occur in the future.

The failure of a tailings storage facility could negatively impact our business, reputation and
results of operations.
Mining companies face inherent risks in their operation of tailings storage facilities. Tailings
storage facilities, such as tailings ponds, are structures designed and managed to contain fine mining
waste, known as tailings. Tailings are a by-product of mining, consisting of the processed rock or soil
left over from separating the commodities of value from the rock or soil within which they occur.
However, the use of tailings storage facilities exposes us to certain risks that could be detrimental to
operations, the environment, and/or public health and safety that may arise from some present process
or future event. Tailings storage facilities designed as upstream raised facilities may present greater
risk, particularly where the facility is located in an area of high seismic activity. When tailings storage
facilities fail, the consequences can be catastrophic for communities, local economies and the
surrounding environment. The occurrence of a tailings dam failure at one of our tailings storage
facilities could also lead to the loss of human life and/or extensive property and permanent
environmental damage, leading to the need for a large expenditure on contingencies and on recovering
− 54 −

=== PAGE 65 ===
RISK FACTORS
the regions and people affected, and the payment of penalties, fines or other monetary damages.
Tailings facilities are in a near-constant state of change, from initial construction, during operations
and until closure. This presents a significant challenge in reviewing and assessing their safety,
requiring a multi-faceted programme with multiple levels of safety assessment in order to be effective.
There can be no guarantee of the effectiveness of our designs or the construction quality of the tailings
storage facilities. There can be no guarantee that the monitoring of the tailings storage facilities would
effectively identify safety concerns either. Nor can there be any guarantee that any of the measures
that have been put in place to safeguard our tailings storage facilities will prevent the failure of one
or more of them, or that such potential failure will be detected in advance.
An increase in the unplanned strip ratio poses significant risks to our mining operations,
particularly in terms of operating costs and overall economic viability.
A higher strip ratio means that more waste material must be removed to access a given quantity
of ore. This results in increased operational costs, including higher expenditures on fuel, labour,
equipment wear and tear, and maintenance. Elevated strip ratios can make certain mining areas
uneconomical, particularly during periods of low commodity prices or rising operational costs. If
product prices decline, the reduced profit margins associated with high strip ratios could significantly
impact our overall profitability.
Moreover, high strip ratios often require substantial upfront capital investments in heavy
equipment, haul roads, and waste storage facilities. These capital outlays can create cash flow
constraints, limiting our ability to fund other critical projects or initiatives. Such financial pressures
may also restrict opportunities for mine expansion, exploration, or the adoption of new technologies,
potentially undermining the long-term competitiveness of our mining operations.
In summary, an elevated strip ratio represents a persistent risk to the financial performance and
operational sustainability of our mining operations. Effective mine planning, cost management, and
operational efficiency are essential to mitigating these risks and ensuring the continued economic
viability of our projects.
Subject to specific geological circumstances, we may be affected by challenges relating to slope
and stability of underground openings.
Unlike open-pit operations, which generally benefit from more straightforward geological
conditions and higher predictability of ore extraction, underground mining involves complex geology
(including faults and folds), higher uncertainty in localisation and reserve estimation, and specialised
systems (ventilation, drainage, hoisting and enhanced ground support) that increase cost and
execution risk. We may adopt new mining techniques following the commercial operation of our
underground mine. The underground mine is to be dug deeper while the waste and tailings deposits
increase in size. Under these circumstances, certain geotechnical challenges may arise, including, for
example, the possibility of failure of the mine’s underground openings or voids, collapses, water
inrush or flooding, ventilation failures and gas explosions, all of which can have consequences, such
as serious safety hazards to workers, regulatory intervention, prolonged disruptions to mining
operations, damage to equipment and infrastructure, and costly remediation and repairs.
− 55 −

=== PAGE 66 ===
RISK FACTORS
The risk of underground mine failure is influenced by various factors, including geological
conditions, the design of the mine, and the methods of extraction employed and is generally higher
than in open-pit mining due to the need for complex support measures (e.g., rock bolts, shotcrete and
metal frameworks) and continuous management of ventilation and drainage systems. As we excavate
deeper, the pressure exerted on the surrounding rock increases, which can compromise the stability
of mine structures. If additional measures are necessary to prevent such failures, it may lead to
unanticipated expenses that can impact our financial performance, reduce production, or necessitate
changes to mine plans. Moreover, the stability of underground openings is crucial not only for
operational safety but also for the integrity of our stated Ore Reserves. Any instability could result
in a reassessment of these reserves, affecting our overall resource estimation and future planning and,
in more severe cases, could result in impairment, write-downs, suspension of operations or closure of
affected areas of the mine.
We have a high concentration of customers during the Track Record Period.
We have a significant concentration of customers during the Track Record Period. For the years
ended 31 December 2022, 2023, 2024 and the seven months ended 31 July 2025, our five largest

entails inherently higher operational complexity, cost intensity and safety risk. In particular,
underground operations require the development and continuous operation of hoisting, ventilation and
drainage systems and extensive ground support; face more complex and variable geological
conditions; and generally exhibit lower certainty and predictability in ore delineation, access and
extraction than open-pit mines. Underground operations are also exposed to acute safety hazards,
including gas explosions, water inrush and collapses, as well as risks arising from ventilation or
drainage failures and ground pressure, any of which can result in prolonged shutdowns, cost overruns,
production shortfalls or severe accidents. That said, it may become possible that we may not be able
to generate profits in the future. We may encounter risks and uncertainties commonly experienced by
some of the mining companies, including those relating to:

method based on the actual production volume over the estimated total proven and probable reserves
of the mines. Estimating reserves involves inherent complexity and uncertainty, relying on geological,
engineering and economic data interpretations. If the mining property is abandoned, the relevant
mining rights are written off in the statement of profit or loss. Exploration and evaluation assets are
stated at cost less impairment losses. Similarly, if any project is abandoned in a very unlikely event,
the total expenditure incurred, including to acquire exploration rights and to carry out exploration
activities, will be written off in our statement of profit or loss. For details, see note 4 of the
Accountants’ Report in Appendix I to this prospectus. Although our intangible assets increased from

evaluation assets may have a material adverse impact on our results of operations.
RISKS RELATING TO CONDUCTING BUSINESS IN THE PRC
We are subject to the political, economic and social development as well as laws, rules and
regulations in the PRC.
Our business is mainly operated in Xizang, the PRC, where we conduct the majority of our
operations. As a result, our business is linked to the political, economic and social climate of the
region and the PRC as a whole, and national and social security to a certain extent. The PRC
Government’s measures to stimulate economic growth and resource allocation have historically
introduced a degree of uncertainty that could potentially impact our operations.
− 67 −

=== PAGE 78 ===
RISK FACTORS
We shall comply with the applicable PRC laws, rules and regulations. With the social
development, the relevant PRC laws, rules and regulations in force at present may be amended in the
future, and their interpretation and implementation shall be determined in accordance with relevant
laws and regulations in force at the time. Any non-compliance with any existing or new laws and
regulations could materially and adversely affect our business, financial condition, results of
operations, cash flows and prospects.
We may be affected by currency exchange regimes and exchange rate fluctuation.
During the Track Record Period, we generated our revenue, expenditures, liabilities and assets
in RMB, while the net proceeds from the Global Offering will be in HKD. Our operations and
financial results are significantly influenced by the fluctuations in currency exchange rates,
particularly between the RMB and the HKD, as well as the USD and other foreign currencies.
Under the current PRC foreign exchange control system, the PRC Government exercises
significant control over the convertibility of RMB into foreign currencies and the remittance of
currency out of the country. The PRC’s foreign exchange control system may impede our ability to
obtain sufficient foreign currency for dividend payments to shareholders, to satisfy any other foreign
exchange requirements, or to capitalise our capital expenditure plans, and even our business operating
results and financial condition.
The PRC Government may also at its discretion restrict access to foreign currencies for current
account transactions in the future. While certain current account transactions can be made in foreign
currencies without prior approval from the State Administration of Foreign Exchange (“SAFE”) by
adhering to existing foreign exchange regulations, converting RMB into foreign currency and
remitting it out of the PRC to pay for capital expenses, such as repaying foreign-denominated debts,
requires government approval. The restrictions on foreign exchange transactions under capital
accounts may also affect our ability to secure foreign exchange through debt or equity financing.
Fluctuations in the value of the Renminbi may have an effect on our business.
Our business may be significantly influenced by variations in the exchange rates between the
RMB and other major currencies, such as the HKD and the USD. As the proceeds raised from the
Global Offering will be expressed in HKD, should the Renminbi strengthen against the USD, the Hong
Kong dollar, or any other foreign currency, there could be a decrease in the value of our assets that
are denominated in those foreign currencies, as well as a reduction in the proceeds from the Global
Offering. On the contrary, weakening of the Renminbi could negatively impact the value of our H
Shares when measured in foreign currency terms, and similarly affect any dividends we declare on
these shares.
In addition, the fluctuations in the value of the Renminbi relative to the HKD or USD would
affect our financial results in HKD or USD terms, even in the absence of any fundamental changes
in our business operations or actual financial performance.

RISK FACTORS
There may be changes regarding the interpretation and enforcement of laws, rules and
regulations where we conduct business.
Our business is subject to the legal and regulatory environment of the PRC. The PRC legal
framework is fundamentally a civil law system, which is characterised by a comprehensive set of
written statutes and regulations. It is important to recognise that many of these laws, rules and
regulations are of recent origin and are subject to continuous interpretations from time to time.
Consequently, the interpretation and enforcement of these legal instruments can vary, leading to a
degree of uncertainty. While the Supreme People’s Court may provide authoritative guidance, the
volume of published court decisions that can be referenced is relatively sparse, and their precedential
value is generally limited. As the PRC’s legal system is characterised by the issuance of new laws,
rules, regulations, guidelines, and interpretations, such changes may at any time retrospectively affect
our existing legal rights, protections and remedies.
It may be difficult to effect service of process, enforce foreign judgments and arbitral awards
against us or our Directors and senior management located in the PRC.
The substantial presence of our operations, assets, and personnel within the PRC jurisdiction has
significant implications for our legal and regulatory landscape. Most of our Directors and senior
management team are residents of the PRC, and their assets are predominantly located within the
PRC. As a result, it presents a challenge in effecting service of process outside of the PRC, including
but not limited to jurisdictions such as the United States or Hong Kong. Consequently, shareholders
may face difficulties in enforcing judgments against our company or its Directors and senior
management team if such judgments originate from courts outside of the PRC.
On 25 January 2024, the Supreme People’s Court of the PRC and the Hong Kong government
entered into the Arrangement on Reciprocal Recognition and Enforcement of Judgments in Civil and
Commercial Matters by the Courts of the Mainland and Hong Kong (關於內地與香港特別行政區法
院相互認可和執行民商事案件判決的安排) (the “Arrangement”). Although theArrangement seeks to
establish a bilateral legal mechanism with greater clarity and certainty for recognition and
enforcement of judgments in a wider range of civil and commercial matters between the courts of
Hong Kong and the PRC, there can be no assurance as to the outcome, effectiveness and enforceability
of the judgements in a PRC court.
Holders of our H Shares are subject to the PRC income tax.
Non-PRC resident individuals and enterprises holding our H Shares are subject to PRC tax laws
and regulations, which impose different tax obligations on dividends received and gains realised from
the sale or other disposition of H Shares.
Non-PRC resident individuals are required to pay a 20% individual income tax on dividends
received and the gains realised upon the sale or other disposition of the H Shares held by them, as
stipulated by the Individual Income Tax Law of the PRC (2018 Revision) (《中華人民共和國個人所
得稅法 (2018 修訂)》) and its implementation regulations. We are required to withhold such tax from
dividend payments, unless applicable tax treaties between the PRC and the jurisdictions in which the
foreign individuals reside, reduce or provide an exemption for the relevant tax obligations. Pursuant
to the Circular of the State TaxationAdministration on Individual Income Tax Collection Issues upon

Abolishment of Document Guoshuifa [1993] No. 045 《( 國家稅務總局關於國稅發[1993]045號文件廢
止後有關個人所得稅徵管問題的通知》), a tax rate of 5% to 20% (generally 10%) shall apply to the
dividends paid by domestic non-foreign-invested enterprises issuing shares in Hong Kong to overseas

As for non-PRC resident enterprises incorporated under the laws of the foreign country whose

Paid to Overseas Non-PRC Resident Enterprise Shareholders of H Shares 《( 關於中國居民企業向境

payable to non-PRC resident enterprise holders of H Shares has been reduced to 10% and we intend
to withhold tax at a rate of 10% from dividends paid to non-PRC resident enterprise holders of our
H Shares (including HKSCC Nominees). Non-PRC resident enterprises that are entitled to be taxed
at a reduced rate under an applicable income tax treaty or arrangement will be required to apply to
the PRC tax authorities for a refund of any amount withheld in excess of the applicable treaty rate,
and payment of such refund will be subject to the PRC tax authorities’ approval.
Given these uncertainties on the interpretation of the PRC tax laws, holders of our H Shares
should consider the potential impact of PRC tax laws on their investment and the possibility of future
changes that could affect the tax treatment of their holdings.
Payment of dividends is subject to conditions under the PRC law.
As stipulated under PRC laws, dividends may be paid only out of distributable profits.
Distributable profits refer to net profit as determined under PRC GAAP or IFRS Accounting
Standards, whichever is lower, less any recovery of accumulated losses and appropriations to statutory
and other reserves that we are required to make. As a result, we may not have sufficient, if any,
distributable profits to enable us to make dividend distributions to our Shareholders in the future,
including periods for which our financial statements indicate that our operations have been profitable.
Any distributable profits that are not distributed in a given year are retained and available for
distribution in subsequent years.
In addition, because the calculation of distributable profits under PRC GAAP is different from
the calculation under IFRS Accounting Standards in certain respects, our subsidiaries may not have
distributable profits as determined under PRC GAAP, even if they have profits for that year as
determined under IFRS Accounting Standards, or vice versa. Accordingly, we may not receive

RISKS RELATING TO THE GLOBAL OFFERING
There has been no prior public market for our H Shares, and their liquidity and market price
may be volatile.
Prior to the completion of the Global Offering, there has been no public market for our H Shares.
The Offer Price range for our H Shares is the result of negotiations between us and the Overall
Coordinators (for themselves and on behalf of the Underwriters), and the Offer Price may differ

assurance that an active and liquid trading market for our H Shares will develop or be sustained after
the completion of the Global Offering. There is also no guarantee that the market price of our H
Shares will not decline following the completion of the Global Offering. Furthermore, the market
price and trading volume of our H Shares may be highly volatile. Factors including but not limited
to our financial condition, actual or anticipated fluctuations in our operating performance,
announcements of competitive developments, acquisitions or strategic alliances in our industry and
general political, financial, social and economic conditions may have a material adverse effect on the
market price and trading volume of our H Shares.
Holders of our H Shares are subject to the risk that the price of our H Shares could fall during
the period before trading of our H Shares begins.
The price of our H Shares sold to the public under the Global Offering will be determined on
the pricing date. However, our H shares will not commence trading on the Stock Exchange until they
are delivered, which is expected to be several business days after the pricing date. As a result,
investors of our H shares may not be able to sell or otherwise deal in our H Shares during that period.
Accordingly, holders of our H Shares may be subject to the risk that our H Share trading price could
fall during the period before trading of our H share begins as a result of adverse market conditions
or other unfavourable developments which arise between the date of sale and the date trading begins.
Future sales orperceived sales of substantial amounts of ourH Shares in the public market could
have a material adverse effect on the prevailing market price of our H Shares and our ability to
raise additional capital in the future.
The market price of our H Shares could be significantly influenced by the sale or the expectation
of the sale of substantial volumes of our H Shares in the public market. Such sales, or the perception
that they might occur, have the potential to cause a material decrease in the market price of our H
Shares. This is particularly relevant when considering the potential issuance of new H Shares or
securities that are convertible into or exchangeable for H Shares.

WAIVERS FROM STRICT COMPLIANCE WITH THE LISTING RULES
In preparation for the Listing, our Company has sought the following waiver from strict
compliance with the relevant provisions of the Listing Rules.
MANAGEMENT PRESENCE IN HONG KONG
Pursuant to Rules 8.12 of the Listing Rules, our Company must have sufficient management
presence in Hong Kong. This normally means that at least two of the executive Directors must be
ordinarily resident in Hong Kong. Rule 19A.15 of the Listing Rules further provides that the
requirement in Rule 8.12 of the Listing Rules may be waived by having regard to, among other
considerations, our arrangements for maintaining regular communication with the Stock Exchange.
Our principal business and operations are located, managed and conducted in the PRC through
its operating subsidiaries established in the PRC. Since the management and operation of our Group
have been mainly under the supervision of our sole executive Director and senior management, our
Company considers that it would be impractical and not commercially necessary for our Group to
appoint additional executive Directors solely for the purpose of satisfying Rules 8.12 and 19A.15 of
the Listing Rules.
Accordingly, we have applied to the Stock Exchange for, and the Stock Exchange has granted,
a waiver from strict compliance with the requirements under Rules 8.12 and 19A.15 of the Listing
Rules, subject to the condition that the following measures and arrangements are made for
maintaining regular, adequate and effective communication with the Stock Exchange:
(i) we have appointed two authorised representatives pursuant to Rule 3.05 of the Listing
Rules, who will act as our principal channel of communication with the Stock Exchange.
The two authorised representatives of our Company (“Authorised Representatives”) are
Ms. He, our sole executive Director who is a permanent resident ordinarily residing in
Hong Kong and Mr. Li Shun, our company secretary and chief financial officer. Each of the
Authorised Representatives will be available to meet with the Stock Exchange within a
reasonable period of time upon the request of the Stock Exchange and will be readily
contactable by telephone and/or email. Each of the Authorised Representatives is
authorised to communicate on behalf of our Company with the Stock Exchange;
(ii) each of the Authorised Representatives has means to contact all members of our Board
(including our independent non-executive Directors) promptly at all times as and when the
Stock Exchange wishes to contact our Directors for any matters. To enhance the
communication between the Stock Exchange, the Authorised Representatives and our
Directors, we have provided the Stock Exchange with the respective office phone number,
mobile phone number and email address of each Director. In the event that a Director
expects to travel or is out of the office, he/she will provide the phone number of the place
of his/her accommodation or other means of communication to the Authorised
Representatives;

services, and industry conferences for the metals and mining sector. With over 20 years of experience,
SMM comprehensively addresses diverse metal markets. Headquartered in Shanghai, SMM operates
subsidiaries in Yantai, Foshan, Beijing, Chengdu, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, and internationally in
Singapore, the UK, Indonesia, and the US. Employing over 500 professionals globally, SMM
publishes daily Shanghai spot prices (SMM prices) for hundreds of nonferrous metal products,
establishing itself as an authoritative source for contract settlements. These prices comply with
IOSCO international standards, making SMM the only third-party pricing agency in China’s
nonferrous industry certified by IOSCO. SMM has received multiple accolades, including recognition
as a National High-Tech Enterprise and Shanghai Innovative Small and Medium-sized Enterprise.
SMM conducted both primary and secondary research using a variety of resources. Primary
research involved interviewing key industry experts and leading industry participants. Secondary
research involved analysing data from various publicly available data sources, such as National
Bureau of Statistics of China, United States Geological Survey, etc. In compiling the SMM Report,
SMM has adopted the following of each market: (i) the social, economic and political environment

INDUSTRY OVERVIEW
OVERVIEW OF ZINC INDUSTRY
Zinc Industry Value Chain
The zinc industry value chain is similar to that of lead. Zinc ore is extracted and processed into
concentrates. Upstream mining companies generally sell concentrates to traders, who conduct onward
sales to refineries. Refineries refine the concentrates into ingots. Downstream enterprises further
process the ingots into products like galvanised sheets, alloys, and zinc oxide. These processed zinc
derivatives are ultimately utilised across industries such as real estate, automotive, and infrastructure.
In 2024, China’s domestic consumption of refined zinc reached 6,642.0 kt. Infrastructure and
construction represented the predominant consumers, accounting for approximately 34.0% and 22.0%
of total consumption, while transportation and consumer durable together contributed 30.0%.
Intermediate Processing
Source: SMM
Zinc Reserves
Zinc is a light grey, conductive metal that is abundant in the Earth’s crust. Global zinc reserves
in 2024 were approximately 230,000.0 kt. The top 3 countries accounted for approximately 60.4% of
the global zinc reserves. Among them, the zinc reserves ofAustralia, China and Russia were 64,000.0
kt, 46,000.0 kt and 29,000.0 kt, respectively. Their global shares were approximately 27.8%, 20.0%
and 12.6%, respectively.
Global Zinc Concentrate Supply and Demand
Regarding supply, from 2018 to 2024, global zinc concentrate production declined at a CAGR
of approximately -1.2%. This trend was influenced by multiple factors, including the extreme weather,
and geopolitical conflicts, etc. Additionally, some mines in countries such as Peru closed or suspended
production due to resource depletion, labour shortages, and strikes, leading to a contraction in global
zinc concentrates supply. However, from 2025 to 2028, with the commissioning of several large
lead-zinc mining projects, the CAGR of global zinc concentrate supply is expected to be 1.8%.
− 93 −

=== PAGE 104 ===
INDUSTRY OVERVIEW
Regarding demand, from 2018 to 2024, global zinc concentrate demand initially increased from
12,711.0 kt in 2018 to 13,111.0 kt in 2021, followed by a decline to 12,362.0 kt in 2024, resulting in
a CAGR of approximately -0.5%. The shortage in the supply of zinc concentrates led to price
increases, prompting downstream enterprises to adopt recycled zinc as a substitute for zinc
concentrates. However, due to the undersupply of recycled zinc raw materials and the immature
market development, the market size of recycled zinc is far smaller than that of primary zinc, making
it highly unlikely for recycled zinc to replace primary zinc in the future. From 2025 to 2028, demand
is expected to rise again, increasing from 12,523.0 kt to 13,005.0 kt, with a CAGR of approximately
1.3%, driven by rising end-use consumption.

Zinc Concentrate Supply and Demand in China
Similar to China’s lead concentrate market, the zinc concentrate market in China is also facing
a supply deficit, as demand for exceeds domestic production, necessitating the import of zinc
concentrate from overseas. From 2018 to 2024, domestic production declined at a CAGR of -2.3%,
caused by the short lifespan of some domestic mines and the instability of ore grades. During the same
period, imports experienced a significant increase to meet downstream demand, with a CAGR of
approximately 5.8%. It is anticipated that from 2025 to 2028, the start-up of new projects will further
enhance supply, with domestic production expected to maintain a CAGR of 2.8%, while the CAGR
of imports will decline to 2.0%.
The demand for zinc concentrates in China continues to rise. As the largest consumer of refined
zinc, China has a significant demand driven by its infrastructure and galvanising industries. It is
anticipated that from 2025 to 2028, demand will increase with a CAGR of 2.2%, due to advancements
in downstream industries.

Zinc Concentrate Price in China
The fluctuation of domestic zinc concentrates treatment charges (“TC”) is influenced by the
supply-demand situation in the zinc concentrate market. Zinc concentrate prices generally have an
inverse relationship with TC. In addition to TC, the pricing of domestic zinc concentrates also
considers the additional profit-sharing mechanism, the “80-20 split”, where the zinc price benchmark
(which has been RMB15,000.0 per tonne for the past decade) is pre-agreed. When the refined zinc
price exceeds or falls below the price benchmark of RMB15,000.0 per tonne, the mine shares or bears
80.0% of the price spread, while the refinery shares or bears 20.0%. When the #1 refined zinc price
is greater than RMB15,000.0 per tonne, the calculation formula is: Zinc concentrate price = SMM 1#
refined zinc price -TC - (SMM 1# refined zinc price - RMB15,000.0) * 0.2; when the SMM 1# refined
zinc price is less than RMB15,000.0 per tonne, the calculation formula is: Zinc concentrate price =
SMM 1# refined zinc price - TC + (15,000 - SMM 1# refined zinc price) * 0.2. Additionally, when
calculating the price of zinc concentrates, the price per tonne needs to be adjusted based on the
benchmark grade. The lower the grade, the greater the price deduction.
Overall, China’s zinc concentrate prices are influenced by the fluctuation of refined zinc prices
and zinc concentrate TC. For example, for zinc concentrates with a grade of 50.0%, from 2018 to
2024, zinc concentrate prices showed a fluctuating trend, dropping from RMB17,788.0 per tonne in
2018 to RMB12,151.0 per tonne in 2020, then rapidly rising to RMB19,073.0 per tonne in 2022. In
2023, due to the significant decline in refined zinc prices, zinc concentrate prices fell back to
RMB15,322.0 per ton. In 2024, with the rise in refined zinc prices and the decline in TC, China’s zinc
concentrate prices rebounded to RMB19,020.0 per tonne. In 2025, due to an increase in imports of
zinc concentrates, domestic zinc concentrate prices are expected to slightly decrease to RMB18,601.0
per tonne. Looking ahead to 2026-2028, influenced by supply-demand relationships, China’s zinc
concentrate prices are expected to show a slight increase followed by a decline, dropping from
RMB18,904.0 per tonne in 2026 to RMB18,848.0 per tonne in 2028.
− 95 −

=== PAGE 106 ===
INDUSTRY OVERVIEW
Currently, zinc concentrate TC prices are mostly determined after negotiations between mines
and refineries. Since TC theoretically represents the processing fee paid by mines to refineries, when
zinc concentrate supply is tight, TC is lower; when zinc concentrate supply is ample, TC is higher.
Since 2018, due to factors such as the global economic slowdown and China-US trade frictions,
downstream zinc demand weakened, and refineries’ demand for zinc concentrate decreased, causing
TC to gradually rise to RMB6,196.0 per tonne in 2019. Subsequently, due to the pandemic, zinc
concentrate production decreased, and TC fell to about RMB4,000.0 per tonne by 2022. In 2023, due
to the overall surplus of domestic zinc concentrate supply, TC remained high, with an annual average
TC of RMB4,929.0 per tonne. By 2024, with the continued tight supply of zinc ore, TC was under
great pressure, dropping to RMB2,642.0 per tonne. In 2025, the increase in imported zinc concentrates
alleviated the domestic supply pressure of zinc concentrate compared to 2024, leading to a rise in TC
to RMB3,434.0 per tonne. Looking ahead, due to downstream demand and continued tight mine
supply, TC is expected to continue to decline slightly from 2026 to 2028. Considering that refineries
have already reached breakeven point, the decline in TC will be limited.

Competitive Landscape in China and Xizang
China is the largest producer of zinc concentrates in the world. However, due to the geographical
distribution of zinc resources and mineralisation conditions, the production of zinc concentrates in
China is dispersed, with most coming from small-scale mines. In 2024, our Company ranked among
theTop 60 zinc concentrate producers in China. The production of zinc concentrates in Xizang in 2024
was approximately 111.3 kt, accounting for 3.1% of the national total, with our Company ranking fifth
in production in Xizang. From 2022 to 2024, the average annual production of zinc concentrates in

OVERVIEW OF LEAD INDUSTRY
Lead Industry Value Chain
The lead industry chain contains mining, smelting, intermediate processing and downstream
applications. Lead ore is mined and processed into lead concentrate, which is then smelted into
refined lead by refineries. Procuring ore from independent third parties occasionally occurs in mining
companies. Upstream mining companies generally sell concentrates to traders, who conduct onward
sales to refineries. Downstream processing enterprises further process refined lead into lead oxide,
lead alloys, etc., to produce lead-acid batteries and other products, which are ultimately used in
industries such as chemicals, automotive and energy storage. In 2024, lead consumption in China was
dominated by lead-acid batteries, which accounted for approximately 86.0% of the total consumption.
Intermediate Processing
Source: SMM
Lead Reserves
Lead is a blue-grey metal with a low melting point, weak ductility, strong malleability, high
corrosion resistance, and the ability to block radiation. Global lead reserves in 2024 were
approximately 96,000.0 kt. The top 3 countries accounted for 68.6% of the global lead reserves,
indicating a high concentration of resources. Among them, the lead reserves of Australia, China and
Russia were 35,000.0 kt, 22,000.0 kt and 8,900.0 kt, respectively. Their global shares were
approximately 36.5%, 22.9% and 9.3%, respectively.
Global Lead Concentrate Supply and Demand
Globally, the production of lead concentrates is mainly concentrated in countries such as China,
Australia, the US, Mexico, and Peru. China is the world’s largest country in lead mine production,
accounting for over 33.0% of lead concentrate supply. The global lead concentrate production
experienced a slight decline, with a CAGR of -0.6% from 2018 to 2024. This downward trend could
be attributed to several critical factors, including the impacts of extreme weather events, geopolitical
tensions and strikes, etc., which led to operational suspensions across various mining sites. It is
anticipated that global lead concentrate supply will gradually recover, increasing with a CAGR of
approximately 1.3% from 2025 to 2028.
− 98 −

=== PAGE 109 ===
INDUSTRY OVERVIEW
During the same period, global lead concentrate demand decreased at a CAGR of -0.5% from
2018 to 2024. Supply shortages of lead concentrates in certain years resulted in price increases,
thereby prompting downstream enterprises to adopt recycled lead as a substitute for lead concentrates.
However, The capacity utilisation rates of recycled lead producers are limited due to raw material
supply constraints, including the tight availability of waste lead-acid batteries and environmental
protection regulations, which restrict the stability of recycled lead supply. The cost of recycled lead
products has approached that of primary products. Therefore, it is highly unlikely that recycled lead
will replace primary lead in the future. From 2025 to 2028, demand is expected to grow steadily at
a CAGR of approximately 0.9%, driven by the growth in end-use consumption.

Lead Concentrate Supply and Demand in China
A supply deficit is gripping China’s lead concentrate market, as demand exceeds domestic
production, necessitating the import of lead concentrate from overseas. From 2018 to 2024, domestic
production grew steadily at a CAGR of approximately 2.0%, supported by the commissioning of new
projects. Except in 2022, when production fell to 1,404.0 kt due to the COVID-19 pandemic and
power rationing. During the same period, imports initially increased and then decreased, with a CAGR
of approximately 0.1%. As domestic production has grown, imports have gradually declined. It is
anticipated that from 2025 to 2028, the start-up of new projects will further enhance supply of lead
concentrate, with domestic production expected to maintain a CAGR of approximately 2.0%, while
imports are projected to decrease at a CAGR of approximately -1.0%. In terms of lead concentrate
demand, due to the influence of the substitution for lead concentrate with recycled lead, the overall
domestic lead concentrate demand has shown a downward trend from 2018 to 2024. However, since
2024, due to the instability of raw material supplies for recycled lead, the production of recycled lead
has begun to decline. It is anticipated that the future impact of recycled lead as a substitute for lead
concentrates will continue to diminish.

Lead Concentrate Price in China
The pricing mechanism for domestic lead concentrates is relatively straightforward, calculated
by deducting treatment charges (“TC”) from the price of #1 refined lead. The price per ton is adjusted
based on benchmark grades, typically 50% or 60%, with greater deductions for lower grades.
Domestic mine prices fluctuate with market conditions but generally respond more slowly than
international prices. The pricing of precious metals in lead concentrates can be done separately, but
it must follow specific standards. If harmful elements exceed the limits, the price of lead concentrates
will be correspondingly reduced.
− 100 −

=== PAGE 111 ===
INDUSTRY OVERVIEW
Overall, China’s lead concentrate prices are influenced by fluctuation of refined lead prices and
TC. For instance, prices for 50% grade concentrates decreased from RMB17,462.0 per tonne in 2018
to RMB12,504.0 per tonne in 2020, driven by an oversupply in the market. However, after 2020, due
to a supply shortage in China’s lead concentrate market, lead concentrates prices began rising,
reaching RMB16,501 per tonne by 2024. From 2025 to 2028, it is anticipated that minor supply
constraints will cause lead concentrate prices to increase gradually from RMB16,678.0 per tonne to
RMB16,825.0 per tonne.
TC for lead concentrates are notably influenced by the supply-demand dynamics of upstream raw
materials. Generally, tighter concentrate supply results in lower TC. Prior to 2020, the domestic lead
concentrate market experienced a higher supply, leading to high and rising TC. However, since 2020,
tightening supply has caused TC to decline to RMB675.0 per tonne by 2024. Future declines in TC
are anticipated due to tight concentrate supply, but the extent will likely be limited due to already low
levels.

OVERVIEW OF COPPER INDUSTRY
Copper Industry Value Chain
Copper has excellent ductility, electrical conductivity and thermal conductivity and is easy to
process. As to the copper’s value chain, the upstream is the mining and beneficiation of copper
concentrates. The midstream is the smelting and refining of copper concentrates or copper scrap and
the downstream is the processing and application of copper. Copper processing products include rods,
bars, tubes, plates, foils, etc. Main downstream applications include construction, power,
transportation, household appliances, electronics and machinery. In 2024, China’s downstream
consumption of copper reached approximately 15,234.0 kt. The power industry was the largest sector,
accounting for about approximately 45.0% of total consumption. Consumer durable represented
15.0%, with household appliances like air conditioners being significant users. Additionally,
transportation, construction, and machinery sectors accounted for approximately 12.0%, 9.0% and
9.0%, respectively.
Intermediate Processing
Recycling System
Source: SMM
Copper Reserves
Copper is a highly conductive metal, with global copper ore reserves estimated to reach
980,000.0 kt in 2024. The top 3 countries accounted for 39.8% of the global copper reserves. Among
them, the copper reserves of Chile, Peru andAustralia were 190,000.0 kt, 100,000.0 kt and 100,000.0
kt, respectively. Their global shares were approximately 19.4%, 10.2% and 10.2%, respectively.
Copper reserves in China were approximately 41,000.0 kt, accounting for 4.2% of the total.
Global Copper Concentrate Supply and Demand
From 2018 to 2024, global copper concentrate production exhibited a consistent upward trend,
achieving a CAGR of approximately 1.9%. This continuous increase was supported by the
commissioning of new projects in global copper mining, such as Julong copper mine, Kamoa-Kakula
copper mine and Mirador copper mine. Looking ahead to the period from 2025 to 2028, driven
continuously by the commencement of new mining projects, it is anticipated that global copper
concentrate supply will continue to expand, maintaining a CAGR of 2.6%.

from downstream industries such as wind power, photovoltaics, and new energy vehicles, global

concentrate import volume is expected to rise, with a CAGR of approximately 3.1%.

Copper Concentrate Price in China
Currently, the pricing of China’s copper concentrates mainly uses the price of #1 refined copper
multiplied by the pricing coefficient, minus fees due to grade differences and impurity excess. The
pricing coefficient of copper varies in different periods, normally fluctuating between 60.0%-95.0%.
Settlement is based on a standard copper content of 20.0%, with the specific calculation formula
being: Copper Concentrate Price = #1 Refined Copper Price × Copper Concentrate Pricing Coefficient
+ Copper Grade Variation Fee.
From 2018 to 2024, driven by robust downstream demand and macroeconomic factors, the price
of China’s copper concentrates rose continuously, from RMB43,560.0 per tonne to RMB69,146.0 per
tonne, with a CAGR of approximately 8.0%. Looking ahead to 2025-2028, due to the tight supply of
copper concentrates, the price is expected to continue to rise slightly, from RMB71,998.0 per tonne
to RMB73,986.0 per tonne.
Regarding the pricing coefficient of domestic copper concentrates, due to the continued tight
supply, the pricing coefficient is expected to rise continuously. However, constrained by the high level
of the domestic pricing coefficient, some refineries are operating at a loss, limiting the potential for
further increases.

CONCENTRATE PRODUCTION COST
In 2024, the average total production cost for mining companies in China was approximately
RMB400.0 per tonne. Labour costs represented the largest component in the production of metal
concentrates, accounting for 29.0% of total costs. In recent years, these costs have escalated due to
inflation and expenditures related to third-party engineering teams. Energy costs constituted 21.0% of
the overall production expenses and have similarly seen an upward trend in recent years. Raw material
costs accounted for 10.0%. The COVID-19 pandemic has adversely affected transportation and other
factors, resulting in increased costs of raw materials, such as explosives, agents, and auxiliary
materials. Furthermore, administrative costs represented 6.0% of total production expenses. Other
costs, which encompass maintenance, depreciation, amortisation, and transportation, accounted for
34.0% of the total production costs.
