BUSINESS
the “Snow Lotus Award” (雪蓮杯) to accredit our tailings pond for the aforementioned “Xizang’s
firsts”. In terms of the industry norm, tailings storage can present operational limitations for many of
the mining companies. See “Business — Production — Tailings” in this prospectus for details relating
to our new tailings pond which is currently under construction. Specifically, the capacity of the
tailings pond limits a company’s mining operations over time. Once the maximum storage capacity
is reached, mining companies must either suspend or reduce mining activities to avoid potential
environmental risks and legal liabilities. Additionally, as the tailings pond approaches its maximum
capacity, the costs of processing and transporting tailings may increase, requiring companies to invest
more in infrastructure and, consequently, raising operational costs. Furthermore, mining companies
must comply with environmental regulations to ensure that tailings management meets the requisite
government standards. Failure to adhere to these regulations could result in fines. Nonetheless, our
robust and extended capacity of our tailings facilities storage infrastructure effectively mitigates these
issues. Our extended tailings facility longevity not only reflects our unwavering commitment to
sustainable mining practices but also positions us with a competitive advantage in the mining industry
where effective tailings management is often a pressing concern for most of the market players. This
allows us to concentrate on optimising our mining operational efficiency and maximising productivity
without the constant pressures and uncertainties associated with limited storage options. Moreover,
our ability to maintain a long-term tailings storage capacity demonstrates our foresight and strategic
planning in resource management. It provides reassurance to the local community that we are
dedicated to responsible mining activities. By mitigating risks associated with tailings, we become
able to invest in further enhancements to our mining operations, knowing that we have a solid
foundation to support our ongoing mining activities.
Our Phase 2 Tailings Pond will backup our tailings absorption capacity. This expansion is not
a mere logistical improvement; it represents a pivotal advancement in our mining operational
capabilities. Our investment in advanced tailings management solutions underscores our proactive
approach to tackling challenges inherent to the mining industry and emphasises our deep-rooted
commitment to environmental stewardship. Where sustainability is increasingly critical, a strategic
development positions us favourably for long-term growth and resilience in today’s mining landscape,
which we believe sets us apart from our competitors who may struggle with inadequate storage
solutions, ensuring that we remain at the forefront among the local competitors while upholding our
ESG commitment.

identify mining types more accurately, enhancing our ability to locate valuable resources efficiently.

BUSINESS
Our Mengya’a Mine
Summary
Our Mengya’a Mine is comprised of an open-pit mine, an underground mine, a base camp
complex, a processing plant, and two tailings ponds (one of which is still under development but it
has been substantially completed). The underground mine is located approximately 3.0 km east of the
open-pit mine. The mine sites are situated at elevations between 5,000.0 and 5,300.0 m asl. The base
camp and processing plant are positioned in a valley about 10.0 km north of the mining sites, at an
elevation of around 4,600.0 m asl. Our tailings ponds are located in a valley 5.0 km west of the base
camp and processing plant, with elevations ranging from 4,600.0 to 5,600.0 m asl. The open-pit mine
and underground mine are surrounded by an exploration licence.
The mine’s deposit type is interpreted as a Pb-Zn(-Cu-Ag) skarn deposit, exhibiting layers or
lenses hosted within Carboniferous-Permian sedimentary rocks. The open-pit mine began production
in 2007. The underground mine has commenced commercial operation since the second quarter of
2025. Ores from Mengya’a Mine can, in aggregate, supply 400.0 kt annually to the processing plant,
which produces zinc, lead and copper concentrates.
Our Mengya’a Mine is located within the eastern part of the LhasaTerrane of the Xizang Plateau.
The Xizang Plateau was formed as a result of closure of the Neo-Tethys Ocean and the collision
between the Indian and Eurasian plates and is characterised by three major suture zones. From south
to north, these are the Indus-Yarlung Zangbo Suture, the Bangonghu-Nujiang Suture, and the
Jinsha-Jiang Suture. These suture zones divide the Xizang Plateau into three distinct
tectonostratigraphic terranes: the Lhasa Terrane, the Qiangtang Terrane, and the Songpan-Ganzi
Terrane. A series of east-west-trending thrust belts have been developed as a result of the combined
effects of the southward subduction of the Meso-Tethys Ocean and the northward subduction of the
Neo-Tethys Ocean. This has given rise to a prominent occurrence of overturned folds and thrusts.
During the India-Eurasia collision, the entire Lhasa Terrane was subjected to a compressive stress
regime, leading to the formation of a series of intersecting east-west trending overthrust faults and
north-south trending tensile faults.

Development of underground mine
Our underground mine has commenced commercial operation since the second quarter of 2025.
We have engaged Chongqing Yitong Mine Construction Engineering Company Limited Xizang

“ChongqingYitong”), an independent third party, to undertake the infrastructure works in connection
with the development of our underground mine. Our Mengya’a Mine can, in aggregate, supply 400.0
kt of ores annually to the processing plant, to produce zinc, lead and copper concentrates. Chongqing
Yitong is also an exploration and mining subcontractor of our Company. See “— Exploration and
Mining Subcontracting Arrangement” in this section for details.
The qualification requirements for mining contractors and subcontractors are the same for
open-pit and underground operations. All mining construction works are subject to the same
qualification regime. Under the prevailing standards, general contracting qualifications for mining
engineering are categorised into four tiers: Special Grade, Grade I, Grade II, and Grade III. The
applicable grade is determined by the scale of mining production capacity, with Special Grade
imposing the highest requirements. Based on our mining capacity limit of 400.0 kt/a, our contractors
are required to hold Grade III qualifications. When selecting mining contractors and subcontractors,
we also took other factors into account, such as the estimated costs, adaptation to high altitude and
candidate’s relevant experience in undertaking similar works, in particular underground mining
projects. Chongqing Yitong, who has undertaken the infrastructure works in connection with the
development of our underground mine, holds a Grade II qualification for general contracting of

According to the PRC Mineral Resources Law, the Regulation for Registering to Explore for
Mineral Resources Using the Block System (礦產資源勘查區塊登記管理辦法) and the Procedures for
Administration of Registration of Mining of Mineral Resources (礦產資源開採登記管理辦法), before
the exploration and mining activities relating to mineral resources can commence, the project
company must first obtain the exploration licences and the mining licences, which generally entitle
the project company to the exploration and mining rights attached to the relevant mining project. The
holder of a mining licence has, among others, the rights to engage in mining activities in the
designated area and within the term prescribed under the mining licence, to conduct exploration
within the designated mining area for the purpose of their own production, to set up production
facilities and amenities within the designated area upon obtaining the relevant approvals in
accordance with the relevant laws and regulations, to sell the mineral products except for those
minerals which are required by the State Council to be sold to designated entities, and to acquire the
land use rights legally based on the requirement of its production and construction.
In connection with aforementioned sales of specific minerals which shall be regulated by the
State Council, the Rare Earth Management Regulations (《稀土管理條例》) (the “Regulation”)
stipulates that the MIIT, along with relevant State Council departments, determines and publicly
announces the rare earth mining and separation enterprises that are allowed to conduct the sales of
those specific minerals. The State Council has classified tungsten, tin, antimony and ion-type rare
earth minerals as specific minerals. These minerals are subject to protective mining, with planned and
unified management from extraction to market sale and export. As we do not sell these specific
mineral products, we are not subject to the Regulations.

BUSINESS
We focus on the mining and beneficiation of ores, utilising flotation processes to produce and
separate zinc, lead and copper concentrates as our main products. During the mineral production
process, the presence of coexistent minerals typically results in small amounts of silver being included
in the concentrates. However, since we are a mining company and do not engage in smelting business,
we are unable to further extract and purify the silver content, which exists in trace amounts within
the sold concentrates. It is a standard practice that silver content is valued once it reaches a certain
threshold. Generally speaking, if there are 100 grams of silver per tonne of concentrate, it will be
priced. However, when silver prices become high, even smaller amounts, such as a few dozen grams,
may also be priced. As at the Latest Practicable Date, we do not have separate sales arrangements for
the coexistent silver.
The above exploration licence was initially issued on 12 July 2004. Our current exploration
licence was extended on 24 June 2024, with a validity period up to 24 June 2026, for a duration of
two years. Pursuant to Xizang Autonomous Region Mineral Resources Exploration and Development
Management Guidelines, where our licence was initially obtained more than 10 years ago, any
extension of the licence shall be for two years. Due to changes in the exploration area, our exploration
licence was amended on 16 February 2025, without altering the expiration date. The current two-year
validity period for the extension of our exploration licence is in line with industry practice and is the
maximum duration stipulated by the effective laws at the time. The current exploration licence held
by us has less than one year of validity remaining because we amended the registrations within the
permitted time during the renewal process.
The above mining licence was initially issued in September 2006. Our mining licence underwent
its fifth extension registration on 25 November 2025, with a validity period to 25 November 2045. Our
mining licence covers both open-pit and underground mines. Our underground mine commenced
commercial operations in the second quarter of 2025. If any of our mines have a residual Ore Reserves
upon expiration of our mining licences, we need to submit a renewal application. Under the relevant
PRC laws and regulations and as advised by our PRC LegalAdvisers, if residual reserves remain after
the term of the mining rights expires, the holders of such mining rights are entitled to apply for
extensions of additional terms.
The renewal mechanism for mining licences does not apply to exploration licences because the
Group was granted the exploration licence many years before the Mineral Resources Law of the
People’s Republic of China (2024 Revision) (the “2024 Mineral Resources Law”) came into effect
on 1 July 2025. For exploration licences that were issued before 1 July 2025, the 2024 Mineral
Resources Law has not yet introduced any specific regulations regarding the number of renewals for
exploration licences that were already in existence before the law was implemented. Therefore, until
new regulations are issued by the state or regional government, Huaxia Mining will continue to follow
the existing rules under XizangAutonomous Region Mineral Resources Exploration and Development
Management Guidelines (《西藏自治區礦產資源勘查開發管理指南》), under which if an exploration
licence has been in place for no less than 10 years, each renewal of the licence will be for a period
of two years. Our exploration and mining licences have remained valid upon renewals without any
administrative obstacles since the commencement of the operation of the Mengya’a Mine.

Infill and Validation Programme
From October to November 2024, we conducted an infill and validation programme aiming to
upgrade the defined resource categories and to validate the historical exploration results, as
recommended by SRK. This programme included 2 diamond twinned holes (SRK001 and SRK002) on
pit bench floor, 3 trenches (TR001 to TR003) on pit bench face and 19 underground channels. Core
drilling was conducted using XY-4 drill rigs. Each drill hole began with a PQ size collar to penetrate
the topsoil, transitioning to HQ size for deeper sections. Core recovery ranged from 95.0% to 100.0%,
with an average recovery of 98.0%. Trench samples collected from pit bench face and underground
channel samples collected in drives were all continuous channel intervals of consistent width, depth
and length of approximately 10.0 cm × 5.0 cm × 1.5 m, channelled either by chisels or saws. A total
of 139 samples were taken and sent to SGS Tianjin Laboratory for determination of Pb, Zn, Cu and
Ag contents.

Management Discussion on Ore Procurement
We procured 20.0 kt of ores from an independent third party (which is Supplier B. See “Business
— Our Supplier, Contractors and Subcontractors — Our Top Five Suppliers” in this prospectus for
details), with the amount of RMB17.0 million in aggregate in 2024. For the seven months ended 31
July 2025, we procured 60.0 kt of ores from Xizang Xinhu Mining Co., Ltd.* (西藏鑫湖礦業有限公
司) (“Xizang Xinhu”), which is an independent third party and under the common control as Supplier
B.
Diversifying our ore resources through external procurement is a strategic initiative aimed at
inherently facilitating cost reduction and enhancing our mining efficiency. Although we did not
procure ores from Supplier B in 2022 and 2023, the decision to procure ores from Supplier B in 2024
was consistent with the aforementioned strategic direction. The external ore procurement was also in
line with our strategy to upgrade our production lines in 2024.
According to SMM, it is generally observed that (i) procuring ores from independent third party
ore suppliers occasionally occurs in the mining industry and thus is not an abnormal market conduct;
(ii) mining companies are currently recognising the importance of diversifying their supply of ores to
mitigate risks associated with supply chain disruptions and fluctuating ore grades from their own
mines; (iii) by sourcing high-grade ores from independent third party ore suppliers, mining companies
can enhance their processing efficiency and ensure that they meet customer specifications
consistently; (iv) the competitive landscape of the mining industry necessitates mining companies to
remain agile and adaptable in terms of supply chain management; (v) by integrating external ore
procurement into their operational strategies, mining companies can leverage additional resources
without the extensive capital investment required for new mine development, which allows mining
companies to capitalise on market opportunities while managing costs effectively.
Our management has specifically evaluated the possibility of diversifying our ore resources
through external procurement going forward based on the following discussions:
(i) the processing phase is crucial in our existing business operation chain, which directly
affects the quality and quantity of our zinc, lead and copper concentrates;
(ii) due to the inherent geological constraints or extraction progress, it may become possible
that our own mines may not consistently provide sufficient ores that meet the required
cut-off grade for our concentrate production, which is out of our control;
(iii) we have a plan to maximise the production capability of our Mengya’a Beneficiation Plant;
and
(iv) by introducing external high-grade ores, we attempt to ensure stable operations of our
processing lines, avoiding downtime caused by insufficient raw materials.

Based on the above, our Directors are of the view that diversifying our ore resources through

consistent product quality, and enhance the position of our Company to meet the increasing market

PRODUCTION
Processing of mined ores and production of metal concentrates takes place at our Mengya’a
Beneficiation Plant. Our processing plant, namely, Mengya’a Beneficiation Plant, was established in
October 2007 and was subsequently put into operation in December 2010. It was designed by Lanzhou
Nonferrous Metallurgical Design and Research Institute Company Limited (蘭州有色冶金設計研究院
有限公司), with an initial daily processing nameplate capacity of 2.0 kt, operating approximately 200
days per year, with an annual ore throughput of 400.0 kt. By 2022, the daily processing nameplate
capacity has reached 3.0 kt due to our renovation and upgrades for our processing plant. Mineral
products processed by our processing plant include zinc concentrates, lead concentrates and copper
concentrates, being our key products sold to our customers.

BUSINESS
With the technologically renovated processing plant, our current processing procedure is
well-structured, including traditional three-stage closed-circuit crushing, two-stage closed-circuit
grinding, copper-lead bulk flotation followed by separation, flotation, zinc flotation, and two-stage

A snapshot of Mengya’a Beneficiation Plant
Beneficiation Process
The beneficiation production process includes blending, crushing, grinding, flotation and
product dewatering. The flotation process consists of copper-lead mixed flotation, zinc flotation, and
copper-lead concentrate separation flotation. All intermediate ores are sequentially returned to the
previous operation. The following flowchart summarises the main steps of the beneficiation process
followed by detailed illustration of each step.
Crushing Flotation
Blending Grinding Dewatering
− 171 −

=== PAGE 182 ===
BUSINESS
Blending
Blending is a crucial process in which mineralised waste is blended with high-grade ore to
optimise overall ore quality such that mineralised waste can also be utilised for concentrate
production. Blending enhances the efficiency of subsequent ore processing and concentrate
production, making it a typical example of comprehensive utilisation.
Crushing
The ore transported from the mine is unloaded into a 120.0 m3 raw ore bin or stockpiled in the
raw ore yard. It is then fed into the primary jaw crusher by a heavy-duty plate feeder at the bottom
of the bin. A traditional three-stage closed-circuit crushing process is adopted. The feed size is less
than or equal to 500.0 mm, and the product size is less than 12.0 mm. The crushed product is
transported by belt conveyors to two 1.5-kt fine ore bins, each corresponding to a grinding-flotation
series.
Grinding
The crushed ore in the fine ore bin is fed into the ball mills by multiple vibrating feeders and
belt conveyors. The grinding process uses a two-stage closed-circuit system, with the crushed ore
ground to a fineness of 70.0-75.0% passing -200.0 mesh (74.0 μm). Stage 1 consists of a grid-type
ball mill and a double-screw classifier forming a closed circuit, while Stage 2 consists of a cyclone
group and an overflow ball mill forming a closed circuit. There are two identical grinding circuits,
and the subsequent flotation is also divided into two corresponding series.
Flotation
The process used is named “copper-lead mixed — separation flotation — zinc flotation”.
First, sulphur and zinc minerals are suppressed such that the copper-lead mixed concentrates can
be separated out. After that, the leftover copper-lead tailings goes through zinc flotation to recover
zinc. In the copper-lead flotation stage, two types of equipment are used: flotation columns and
flotation machines. The flotation column helps recover minerals that float easily, while the flotation
machine uses a series of steps — “1 roughing, 3 cleaning, and 3 scavenging” to extract the more
difficult-to-float copper-lead minerals, which include:
• Roughing: The first step where most of the valuable minerals are separated from the waste.
• Cleaning: The next three steps where the concentrates are purified by removing impurities.
• Scavenging: The last three steps where leftover valuable minerals are recovered.
The concentrates from both the flotation column and machine are combined to form the
copper-lead mixed concentrates.
− 172 −

=== PAGE 183 ===
BUSINESS
Secondly, these copper-lead mixed concentrates go through a separation flotation process, again
using the “1 roughing, 3 cleaning, and 3 scavenging” steps. During this stage, lead is suppressed so
that the process produces separate lead concentrates and copper concentrates.
Finally, the leftover material from copper-lead flotation is processed through the same series of
steps to recover zinc concentrates. Throughout the process, intermediate concentrates are recycled
back to earlier stages to maximise recovery.
Dewatering
Zinc concentrates, lead concentrates and copper concentrates all undergo a two-stage dewatering
process, consisting of thickening and filter pressing, to control the final moisture content of the
concentrate to no more than 9.0%, which is the transportable level. If the moisture content exceeds
9.0%, further drying is carried out in the concentrate storage. All water extracted from the
concentrates is pumped into the beneficiation plant’s high-level water recovery tank. The tailings
discharged from the flotation process contain a high volume of water content, with tailings
concentrations as low as 20.0% to 25.0%, with concentration referring to the proportion of solid
particles in the slurry of tailings. Pumping these water-laden tailings up to 500 metres to a high-level
water recovery tank is both energy-intensive and water-inefficient. Therefore, thickening through
dewatering is essential to reduce operational costs and maximise water recovery. This process
significantly increases the tailings concentration to approximately 38.0% by removing excess water
during thickening. The overflow is pumped into the high-level water recovery tank, where it is
returned to the production process as process water. The underflow is pumped to the tailings storage
facility. The return water from the tailings storage is also conveyed through pipelines into the
high-level water recovery tank in the beneficiation plant.

BUSINESS
Mineralised Waste and Comprehensive Utilisation
Mineralised waste refers to material obtained during our mining process that cannot be
economically processed due to low metal content, i.e., bearing a grade that is below the cut-off grade.
In the mining industry, mineralised waste are commonly simply referred as waste.
We adopt the methodology of comprehensive utilisation for mineralised waste that have been
obtained for our mining operations, as it is economically and practically beneficial to recover valuable
components from the mineralised waste, following the introduction of beneficiation process.
mineralised waste can, notably, be blended with high-grade ores such that these mineralised waste can
be economically and rationally used for ore processing and concentrate production. Such processing
is classified as blending in the mining industry, which facilitates the recovery of valuable components
from mineralised waste. Advanced flotation techniques can extract usable components such as metals
from mineralised waste, while chemical leaching can efficiently recover trace amounts of precious
metals or rare earth elements. During the Track Record Period, the mineralised waste we obtained
from our mining process had been used for blending, or kept in our mining site.
In terms of open-pit mining, ores are naturally layered and mixed with waste rocks and stones
beneath the surface. mineralised waste coexist and are often interspersed with higher-quality ores in
complex geological formations. Due to this natural layering, it is inevitable that mining operations
encounter mineralised waste during extraction. The volume of mineralised waste mined depends
largely on the specific and complex geological conditions at each site and depth, rather than on mining
plans or human control. Therefore, the mining team cannot fully control how much mineralised waste
must be removed or processed before reaching higher-quality ore. During the Track Record Period,
fluctuations in the volume of mineralised waste reflected such geological complexities. For example,
in 2024, the mining team encountered less mineralised waste but more pure waste rock, whereas in
2022 and 2023, there was a higher proportion of mineralised waste relative to waste rock.
Mineralised waste contain lower concentrations of economically valuable metals, making them
uneconomical to process on their own. To address this, we have deployed a blending technique,
mixing mineralised waste with higher-grade ores to create an ore blend that meets or exceeds the
processing plant’s minimum threshold. This allows the metal content in mineralised waste to be
recovered effectively, thereby increasing total concentrate output.
Blending is a widely used practice in the mining industry as it maximises metal recovery and
improves overall resource utilisation. We can increase total production volume by incorporating
mineralised waste, which contributes to higher revenues and profits while spreading operational costs
over a larger output. Aside from the increased volume and corresponding revenue growth, the
blending of mineralised waste does not negatively affect the selling price, product quality, or profit
margins of the concentrates compared to those produced solely from higher-grade ores.

BUSINESS
According to Article 7 of the Mineral Resources Law of the PRC, a policy of unified planning,
rational layout, comprehensive exploration, rational exploitation, and comprehensive utilisation for
mineral resources exploration and development is implemented by the State. Xizang Autonomous
Region’s Natural Resources Department (西藏自治區自然資源廳) defines mineralised waste as
minerals that fall between the boundary and lowest industrial grades, lacking mining value under
current economic conditions. Additionally, the Circular Economy Promotion Law 《( 循環經濟促進
法》) requires mining companies to extract and utilise valuable coexistent minerals while preventing
resource loss; and the Draft Implementation Regulations for the Mineral Resources Law of the PRC
(《中華人民共和國礦產資源法實施條例(徵求意見稿)》) emphasises efficient use of mineralised
waste. Based on the above, the comprehensive use of mineralised waste by mining companies does
not contravene the mandatory provisions of the applicable PRC laws and regulations and the relevant
local laws and regulations of Xizang. During the Track Record Period, we consumed approximately
204.7 kt, 217.0 kt, 11.4 kt and nil of mineralised waste to blend with ores economically and
strategically to produce feed ores that meet the specifications for concentrate production purpose. The
mineralised waste that were comprehensively used in our production in 2024 was substantially lower
than that of in 2022 and 2023. Variations in the quantity of mineralised waste that were
comprehensively used each year during the Track Record Period was resulted from the reduction of
the total quantity of ores that were mined from our open-pit mine.
Expansion and technology renovation of Mengya’a Beneficiation Plant
The expansion and renovation of our processing plant started in 2017, and by 2022, the
nameplate daily processing capacity has reached 3.0 kt. The following timeline sets out the milestone
by year in terms of our renovation and upgrades for Mengya’a Beneficiation Plant.
Year Milestone
2017 The crushing system was upgraded by replacing the secondary and tertiary cone
crushers and adding a vibrating screen before secondary crushing, which reduced
the particle size of the crushed product.
2018 Aflotation column was added before the copper-lead mixed flotation to extend the
flotation time and improve copper-lead recovery. Additionally, one more filter
press was added for dewatering the lead and zinc concentrates.
2020 The number of flotation cells for copper-lead rough flotation and zinc rough
flotation was increased from 4 to 6. The scavenger flotation cells were also
adjusted to extend the flotation time.
2021 The reagent system underwent a significant adjustment, drastically reducing lime
consumption. The pH of the process water was reduced from 13-14 to 7-8, leading
to a gradual improvement in beneficiation performance.
2022 The secondary grinding cyclone classifier was replaced from FX500 to FX400, and
the grinding fineness increased from 65.0-70.0% passing 74.0μm to 70.0-75.0%
passing 74.0μm. The copper-lead separation process added a rough flotation cell,
along with an additional scavenger and cleaner flotation stage, which improved the
copper-lead separation efficiency.

(4) The permitted annual ore mining volume and the designed processing volume for the entire year ending 31
December 2025 is 400 kt. The permitted annual ore mining volume and designed processing volume for seven
months ended 31 July 2025 represents the pro rata amount for such period.
(5) The volume is calculated as at 31 July 2025.
The permitted annual mining capacity of our Mengya’a Mine is stipulated as 400.0 kt. We strive
to achieve this volume each year to maximise profitability, which is subject to certain factors, such
as the ore inventory level. That is because an excessive ore inventory not only occupied the limited
storage space but also potentially affected the liquidity position if existing ore inventory were not
converted into operating cash inflow in time through sales. In addition, the extraction of mineralised
waste is common during our mining process. For instance, in 2022, we had a high level of ore
inventory at the beginning of the year, together with large amount of extracted mineralised waste. If
we had carried out the mining plan at full capacity of 400.0 kt whilst keeping its excessive ore and
mineralised waste storage, that would have sunk more cost hence adversely affecting our liquidity
position. Nor was there enough storage space available to accommodate those extra mined ores .
Additionally, the comprehensive utilisation of mineralised waste is promoted and encouraged by the
government to prevent resource loss. Therefore, we adjusted and allocated our processing capacity to
the existing ore inventory together with mineralised waste in 2022 and thus consequentially led to a
reduction in our actual ore mining volume in the year.
The aforesaid reason also applies to 2024. Nonetheless, other factors such as our initiative to
undertake maintenance and technical upgrades to prepare for processing ores from our underground
mines, and the delay in the commencement of mining operations and production timeline due to the
extreme weather conditions in early 2024, also impacted our actual ore mining volume for the year.
By contrast, the combined impact of all the aforesaid factors was minimal in 2023, and
accordingly, we succeeded in reaching an actual ore mining volume of approximately 400.0 kt in
2023.

Tailings
Phase 1 Tailings Pond
The processing plant’s tailings pond, also referred to as Phase 1 Tailings Pond, is located 5.1 km
southwest of the plant on the left bank of the Anong Qu tributary. This valley-type pond has a
designed final stacking elevation of 5,036.0 m asl, a total dam height of 76.0 m, and a storage capacity
of 2.97 million m3. It commenced trial operation in June 2011, with a seepage control modification
implemented in 2014, which included the installation of geotextile membranes.
The initial rock-fill dam features upstream and downstream slopes of 1:2.0, a 12.5 m-wide crest,
and an initial height of 40.0 m, with an additional 36.0 m added through tailings stacking. A 1.5
mm-thick HDPE geomembrane is installed in the pond for seepage control, and drainage facilities
guide seepage water to a return water pool. The catchment area is 4.83 km2, covering 12.6 hectares,
and includes flood diversion ditches to manage rainwater.
Tailings from the flotation plant are concentrated and dewatered before being pumped through
high-pressure pipelines to the pond. Clarified water and seepage are directed back to the plant for
recycling via a gravity-fed pipeline. The pond is equipped with comprehensive monitoring systems for
safety and environmental protection, including rainfall and displacement monitoring facilities, video
surveillance and groundwater environmental monitoring wells. By virtue of construction and
subsequent modifications, the pond has been operated in its normal status, meeting all safety and
environmental standards, with an estimated remaining storage capacity sufficient for another two
years, based on our current actual production volume each year during the Track Record Period.
− 181 −

=== PAGE 192 ===
BUSINESS
Phase 2 Tailings Pond (our new tailings pond)
With the expansion of the mine resource exploration, the proven resource reserves have
gradually increased. As we plan to expand the mining capability, we are of the view that Phase 1
Tailings Pond will no longer meet the tailings discharge requirements after the expansion. To maintain
normal mine ore processing and ensure sustainable development, we have decided to construct a new
tailings pond in another tributary upstream of the Anong Qu, located northeast of Phase 1 Tailings
Pond. As at the Latest Practicable Date, the construction of our new tailings pond had been
substantially completed.
Phase 2 Tailings Pond is administratively located within the jurisdiction of Rongdoi Township,
Jiali County, and is adjacent to Phase 1 Tailings Pond. The straight-line distance between the tailings
dams of the two ponds is about 1.05 km, and the distance from the processing plant is approximately
5.6 km. The new tailings pond is a valley-type pond with a designed final stacking elevation of
5,210.0 m. The total dam height is 153.0 m, with an initial dam height of 53.0 m and a later tailings
stacking dam height of 100.0 m. The total storage capacity of Phase 2 Tailings Pond is 21.2 million
m3, and the effective storage capacity is 13.78 million m3. The total storage capacity of the tailings
pond represents the full geometric volume of the impoundment, while the effective storage capacity
reflects the actual usable space available for tailings deposition after considering essential safety and
operational requirements. According to SRK, at the current flotation plant capacity of 400.0 kt/a, the
estimated service life of Phase 2 Tailings Pond is approximately 64 years, which is sufficient to cover
the LOM of our Mengya’a Mine.

the construction of the new tailings pond. Xizang Jiwei was engaged by us pursuant to our bidding
protocol, which was in full accordance with Bid Invitation and Bidding Law of the PRC 《( 中華人民
共和國招標投標法》).

SALE OF CONCENTRATES
Sales Master Agreement
In spite of customer type, we adopt a standard sales master agreement. The following table sets
out the key terms and conditions of our sales master agreements.
Grade : For lead and zinc concentrates, impurity contents must not exceed
standard limit of each type of concentrates as prescribed in the
sales agreement. For copper concentrates, there is no standard limit
for impurity contents, and the grade would affect the price of the
concentrates.
Delivery : We are responsible for delivering concentrates from our processing
plant to Lhasa upon completion of production. Customers need to
make further arrangements to transport the concentrates from
Lhasa to their designated places.
Sample check : Each of our customers will conduct onsite sampling and moisture
and testing testing on the concentrates to be transported, along with the
issuance of a test report. Samples will also be transported to the
laboratory of our Company for further assessment.
Inspection : Concentrates should be weigh bridged by our Company, in
accordance with the scale standard promulgated by the National
Bureau of Measurement (國家計量局).
− 193 −

=== PAGE 204 ===
BUSINESS
Payment : A deposit of an amount requested by our Company should be
prepaid to us by the customer. Such advance payment is used to
settle the fees of the concentrates ordered by our customers, based
on the corresponding average selling price and the sales amount.
Whilst the deposit for a specific customer falls short of RMB1.0
million, the customer shall top up the deposit, before we deliver
the concentrates to our customers. The remaining deposit shall be
returned to the customer in a situation where the customer’s
demand for the concentrates surpasses our supply.

Non-competition between Recycled Products and our Concentrates
There is currently no direct competition between Recycled Products and our metal concentrates
due to several factors, including lower product quality, lower supply stability, diminishing price
advantages, and technical adaptation barriers in relation to the Recycled Products. See “Industry
Overview — Limitations on the Future Development of Recycled Products” in this prospectus for
details.
Beyond these inherent limitations, the recycled lead sector in China is a well-established
industry with stable and long-standing market players. As a mature and entrenched industry sector, it
is neither new nor emerging, and thus does not pose direct competition to us. As advised by our PRC
Legal Advisers, there are no prevalent relevant PRC laws, regulations or policies that require
downstream industry players to utilise Recycled Products.
Pricing
In China, the market pricing of zinc, lead and copper concentrates is influenced by several
guiding mechanisms rather than being solely determined by market forces. The metal market
references domestic benchmark prices, particularly from SMM, providing a foundation for domestic
pricing. Additionally, industry associations regularly publish reference prices and market trend
reports to assist producers and buyers in their negotiations. Government policies are equally
important. For instance, tariffs on certain metal exports can impact international prices. While these
guiding mechanisms are important, the actual selling price is influenced by market supply and
demand, especially during periods of volatility. Contract negotiations between the seller and the buyer
eventually determine the final selling price, incorporating formulas that reflect market price
fluctuations.

Revenue Recognition
Revenue from our sale of zinc, lead and copper concentrates is recognised at point in time when
control of the concentrates are transferred to our customers, i.e., when the nonferrous metal
concentrates are delivered to the designated locations instructed by our customers, and at prices
pre-determined in the sales master agreements, or a purchase order. We receive payments in advance
from all customers with no credit terms on sales. Contract liability is recognised for sales receipts in
which revenue has yet been recognised. For each sale, a sample of the nonferrous metal concentrates
is inspected by us prior to delivery for the purpose of determining the mineral content to be adopted
as the basis of calculation of transaction price.
Product Delivery
According to our sales master agreements, we are obligated to deliver the concentrates to our
customers, upon the completion of inspection, sample check and testing of our concentrates.
Concentrates are delivered from our processing plant to Lhasa. Customers need to make further
arrangements to transport the concentrates from Lhasa to their designated places.

SEASONALITY
Our mining activities need to be conducted considering the unique weather conditions of Xizang
to optimise operational efficiency and production scheduling. Xizang has distinct plateau climate
characteristics, including significant temperature variations between day and night and well-defined
rainy and dry seasons. In terms of mining activities, summer (i.e., June toAugust) is the optimal time
for exploration and mining activities, as temperature is more pleasant, facilitating our employees’
adaptation to the plateau environment and improving productivity. There is typically a lapse of time
between our exploration and mining operations. Once these phases are initiated, the production of
concentrates occurs continuously throughout the year. However, weather in Xizang can be highly
unpredictable and prone to extreme changes, including heavy rain, sleet, and hail, which may cause
delays to both our mining operations and delay in production schedules at our processing plant. Such
unpredictabilities brought by the extreme weather conditions of Xizang poses uncertainties to our
mining schedule accordingly, differing from other mining companies operating in other regions in the
PRC.
However, during the rainy season spanning from June to August, there may be heavy rain, sleet
and hail, therefore, we must take precautions to address potential risks of slippery roads and
mudslides, ensuring safe and stable logistics transport. Winter, spanning from November to March or
April, presents extreme cold, with ground freezing or being covered in snow, which increases
extraction difficulties and costs, making it generally unsuitable for large-scale mining operations.
March to May generally offers favourable conditions, with less rainfall or snowfall, making it
an ideal time to commence mining operations. This period with relatively stable weather allows for
a smoother start to the mining season, helping to mitigate potential disruptions caused by the region’s
unpredictable climate.
OUR CUSTOMERS
Overview
During the Track Record Period, customers of our zinc, lead and copper concentrates, as
recognised in our financial statements, were nonferrous metal traders who generally blend
concentrates to produce customised concentrates and conducted onward sales of such customised
− 198 −

=== PAGE 209 ===
BUSINESS
concentrates to end users of concentrates, which are refineries to further process the concentrates
depending on their customers’ needs. The downstream refinery customers cover various regions in
China, and most of them are listed companies and/or state-owned enterprises. Refineries refine zinc,
lead and copper concentrates into metal ingots.
It is a common practice in the industry for mining companies, including the Group, to engage
metal traders as intermediaries rather than conducting direct sales to refineries for the following
reasons:
(i) mining companies and refineries have structurally divergent payment preferences. Mining
companies, including the Group, typically prefer payment-before-delivery terms to ensure
liquidity and to finance continuous mining activities and mitigate volatility and default risk. The
payment-before-delivery arrangement is the industry norm, which is common when selling
concentrates to nonferrous metal traders in the demand-driven metal-mining industry. In
contrast, refineries tend to purchase concentrates on delivery-before-payment or extended credit
terms to align their cash collections from downstream metal sales. Metal traders bridge this
fundamental timing mismatch by assuming the intervening funding obligation. They monetise
the concentrates inventory and absorb the refinery’s credit exposure, thereby allowing both the
mining companies and the refineries to avoid incremental working-capital financing that would
otherwise arise in a direct sale arrangement. For these reasons, some refineries even proactively
require mining companies to enter into contracts with their designated metal traders.
(ii) besides liquidity management, metal traders perform an important concentrates consolidation
and blending function that neither mining companies nor refineries can replicate on a
cost-effective basis. Each refinery’s smelting process is calibrated to specific blends of metal
content, impurity levels, and moisture. Traders can pool concentrates from multiple mines with
differing grades and contents and formulate blended concentrates that satisfy the precise
metallurgical specifications of each refinery. If the Group or any mining company were to sell
directly to refineries, the refineries would have a very limited selection scope of mining
company suppliers whose product could directly and completely match the smelting needs of the
refineries; and the refineries must negotiate with one or more mining companies to test, and
manage stockpiles from multiple sources simultaneously, increasing its operational complexity
and costs, inventory-management cost, and quality-control risk.
(iii) metal traders also play a crucial role in solving the problem of logistics and transportation
between the mining companies and refineries, in compliance with national environmental
protection regulations. The production of outputs classified as high-emission under the
“Guidance on Strengthening the Ecological and Environmental Source Control of
High-Energy-Consuming and High-Emitting (Dual-High) Construction Projects” (EIA [2021]
No. 45) is prohibited in Xizang. Consequently, refineries must be located in inland Chinese
provinces, necessitating the long-distance transportation of metal concentrates out of Xizang.
The mining companies such as the Group typically only agree to deliver the concentrates to the
designated locations within a limited distance in Xizang whereas the refineries usually demand
direct delivery to their facilities. This is where metal traders step in, bridging a logistical gap
− 199 −

=== PAGE 210 ===
BUSINESS
to ensure the smooth operation of the entire supply chain. As illustrated above, metal traders do
far more than act as mere resellers of the Group’s products. Instead, they blend concentrates to
produce customised feedstock that aligns with the exact metallurgical specifications of each
refinery.
To the best knowledge of our Directors and upon all reasonable enquiries, there were nonferrous
metal trader customers which are the trading arms of the groups conducting their ore-refining business
via affiliated companies in their same groups. For the purpose of clear presentation, such customers
are classified as a refinery for the avoidance of doubt.

Our Top Five Customers
The lead and zinc mining industry operates in a demand-driven market characterised by
constrained supply that has persisted for many years. Under these conditions, it is generally the
purchasers who initiate contact with mining companies, rather than the other way round, and such
contacts are most often facilitated by industry referrals to companies regarded as credible and
reputable. Moreover, prominent industry gatherings, including the annual China (Shanghai)
International Non-Ferrous Metals Industry Exhibition and the SMM Metal Industry Conference, serve
as indispensable forums through which mining companies, traders, refineries and research institutions
exchange information and cultivate commercial opportunities. The Group, with an operating history
of nearly two decades in Xizang, one of China’s most resource-rich regions for lead, zinc, and copper,
has accordingly achieved broad recognition in the marketplace.
For the years ended 31 December 2022, 2023, 2024 and the seven months ended 31 July 2025,
our top five customers in each year/period accounted for approximately 93.9%, 90.1%, 88.1% and
81.7% of our total revenue, respectively. Our largest customer in each year/period accounted for
approximately 41.0%, 24.2%, 31.2% and 40.8% of our revenue for the years ended 31 December 2022
and 2023, 2024 and the seven months ended 31 July 2025, respectively. We generally conduct
background searches of potential customers to ensure that they are reliable business counter-parties
before we enter into the sales master agreements with these potential customers. According to the
payment term as stipulated in the sales master agreements, a deposit of an amount requested by our
Company should be prepaid to us by the customer.

Impact of co-existent component of silver on the average selling prices
The average selling prices of our lead and copper concentrates are higher than the average
selling price of lead concentrates and copper concentrates in China because the lead and copper
concentrates sold by the Group contained co-existent component of silver. During the mineral
production process, the presence of co-existent minerals typically results in small amounts of silver
being included in the concentrates. However, since the Group is a mining company and does not
engage in smelting business, the silver component was technically unviable to be extracted and
purified during the ore processing and concentrates production processes from lead or copper
concentrates and could only be extracted and purified by further smelting process by the refinery
companies. Therefore, the Group had to price the silver within its lead or copper concentrates.
According to SMM, the average selling prices of 2# silver ingots (99.95%) for the three years ended
31 December 2024 and for the seven months ended 31 July 2025 were RMB4,695.34/kg,
RMB5,537.52/kg and RMB7,201.24/kg, and RMB8,266.35/kg respectively. For the three years ended
31 December 2024 and for the seven months ended 31 July 2025, there were approximately 12.4
tonnes, 18.6 tonnes, 4.2 tonnes and 8.9 tonnes of silver in the lead and copper concentrates which
− 206 −

=== PAGE 217 ===
BUSINESS
attributed to approximately RMB41.7 million, RMB74.7 million, RMB22.5 million and RMB58.1
million in revenue. Due to the much higher price of silver, the Group’s overall selling prices for lead
and copper concentrates had therefore been elevated accordingly depending on the actual amount of
silver component contained in the lead or copper concentrates sold to the relevant customers.
Since the silver component was only co-existent element with the lead and/or copper and only
accounted for approximately 0.1% per ton of the Group’s lead or copper concentrates, additional
revenue generated from silver was grouped under the revenue from sales of lead or copper
concentrates, even though the silver component was priced and charged to the customers on a
standalone basis.
Silver has a strong geochemical affinity for lead and copper due to similar chemical behavior
during ore formation. It often substitutes for lead in galena and integrates into copper ores like
chalcopyrite due to compatible crystal structures and ionic properties. In contrast, silver rarely
co-exists with zinc, as zinc forms distinct minerals like sphalerite that are less compatible with silver.
Silver is typically recovered as a by-product from lead and copper concentrates, while its
concentration in zinc concentrates is usually too low to justify recovery.
The average selling price of our lead and copper concentrates excluding silver are consistent
with the prevailing market trends.
High customer concentration
We have a high concentration of customers during theTrack Record Period. As the zinc, lead and
copper concentrates we sell are large in terms of quantity, we generate our revenue from a limited
number of customers, and most of our top five customers are nonferrous metal traders who generally
conducted onward sales of our concentrates. Accordingly, we had a high concentration of customers
during theTrack Record Period. Our Directors believe that the high concentration of customers during
the Track Record Period will not result in a material adverse impact on our business operations, as
zinc, lead and copper concentrates market is generally defined as a typical demand-over-supply
market in the mining industry, according to SMM. Specifically, we do not depend on downstream
customers for the sale of concentrates to generate profit. Instead, our customers have to actively
secure their supply of concentrates as early and extensively as possible, which is demonstrated by our
balance of our contract liabilities and refundable receipt on our financial statements.
Additionally, we can easily switch and choose new trading partners without compromising our
business interests. Most of our existing customers have had trading relationships with us for years and
had formed trustful business relationship with us with good track record. Importantly, there is no
indication that any of the majority of these customers would like to terminate the business relationship
with us.
Furthermore, our customer portfolio has been gradually diversifying over the past few years,
with the percentage of the top five customers diluting each year. Therefore, our Directors are of the
view, and the Joint Sponsors concur, that the high level of customer and supplier concentration is not
expected to materially adversely impact our business operations.
− 207 −

=== PAGE 218 ===
BUSINESS
Industry norm and relationship stability
Our Directors are of the view and the Joint Sponsors concur that, the likelihood of any material
adverse change or termination of our Group’s relationships with its major customers is remote,
considering that as SMM has confirmed, a high level of customer concentration is an industry-wide
norm in China’s mining sector, not a geographically limited phenomenon. This is primarily because
in our industry customers typically place orders in large volume, unlike small, frequent purchases
from multiple buyers typically of other industries. These customers are stable, long-standing clients
who, in a seller’s market of our industry, are motivated to maintain sizable procurement programmes
to secure reliable supply. Consequently, the Group’s business relationship with top customers is
expected to remain stable. The relationships are mutually beneficial as the Group provides customers
with consistent product supply, while customers provide the Group with stable revenue.
OUR SUPPLIERS, CONTRACTORS AND SUBCONTRACTORS
During the Track Record Period, in conducting our mining operations, we purchased
consumables and public utilities in connection with exploration, mining and processing of ores. In the
normal course of our mining operations, we also procured contracting and subcontracting services
from independent third parties for mining services, transportation services and construction services
in respect of our mining assets such as our underground mine and tailings storage facilities.
During the Track Record Period and up to the Latest Practicable Date, we did not experience any
material lack of capacity, supply shortage, fluctuation in procurement price, delay or disruption in our
business operations relating to our suppliers or any material product claims attributable to our
suppliers or subcontractors.
Suppliers of Consumables and Public Utilities
During the Track Record Period and up to the Latest Practicable Date, we mainly procured
consumables such as mining related devices and relevant parts, reagents, explosives and public utility
such as electricity. We take into consideration a number of factors when selecting our preferred
consumables suppliers. These factors include quality of materials, proximity, safety, and delivery time
and price competitiveness. Our mining operations require us to procure explosives and therefore, our
quality control department places a strong emphasis on the safety and quality of these materials to
ensure our mining operations are in full compliance with the relevant PRC laws and regulations.
Historically and during the Track Record Period, there was no accident relating to the use of
explosives. During theTrack Record Period and up to the Latest Practicable Date, supply of electricity
also remained stable and sufficient for our mining operations, and there had been no incident of
insufficient supply of electricity or blackout that disrupted our mining operations. As our supplier of
electricity is a state-owned enterprise, the electricity price is subject to government pricing and
guidance, Therefore, the electricity is charged at market rate. In addition, there are alternative local
suppliers of consumables, equipment and subcontracting services on comparable prices and terms in
Xizang where the Group operates.

ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL AND GOVERNANCE
We strive to improve our environmental, social and governance (“ESG”) strategies to create an
efficient and diversified production environment. We place ESG principles at the core of our strategy
and continuous enhancements across our operation.
Our ESG Policies and ESG Working Group
We operate our business in a responsible and sustainable manner, and we are committed to
maintaining transparency and accountability to our stakeholders, including but not limited to
employees, communities, customers and suppliers. We believe that our business operations should
abide strictly by the environmental protection regulations of the PRC when dealing with wastes, water
usage and pollutant emissions at our operation sites. We also aim to keep abreast of changes in
government policies and liaise with local regulators to ensure our strict compliance with relevant laws
and regulations. To manage sustainability efforts more effectively, we review, and assess the
effectiveness of our ESG frameworks on a regular basis and have formulated the relevant ESG
policies for our Company.
We have established a Sustainability and Risk Management Working Group (“ESG Working
Group”), which is oversighted by our Board and led by our executive Director. We aim to minimise
our impact on the environment and natural resources in our business operations and monitor and
manage our use of resources, including energy, water and construction materials at operation sites. We
also aim to ensure that wastes are handled in compliance with applicable laws and regulations, thereby
providing a safe, diverse and inclusive workplace for our employees. In addition, we provide regular
training, as well as fair and competitive supports and welfare for our employees.
Our ESG policies mainly include environmental protection policies, mine land reclamation plan
(《礦山地質環境保護與土地復墾方案》), human resources policies, occupational health and safety
policies, operation management policies and business ethics policies and rules, which provide
important guidance for our sustainability practices, allow us to oversee the implementation of ESG
measures and demonstrate our commitment to business integrity, talent development, environmental
protection and community development.
To implement our ESG policies more effectively, we have set up the ESG Working Group
consisting of different members coming from various departments of our Group, including but not
limited to Finance Department, Operation Department, Audit and Legal Department. Our ESG
Working Group possesses rich professional management capabilities in safety, environmental
protection and occupational health. Our ESG Working Group also has comprehensive management
capabilities and a strong sense of responsibility in fulfilling social responsibilities, operating in
accordance with laws and regulations and managing community relations. Our ESG Working Group
holds regular meetings to discuss ESG, internal control and risk management-related matters and
receives reports from relevant departments, and submits reports to our Board for evaluation on a
regular basis. Our Board reviews risks and opportunities relating to sustainability with the ESG
Working Group and approves ESG-related business strategies. Additionally, our Directors will
promptly make resolutions on ESG-related issues raised by the ESG Working Group, formulate work
plans and assign relevant tasks for follow-ups by the relevant departments and/or working units.

BUSINESS
Specifically, our ESG Working Group is responsible for (i) dealing with ESG, internal control
and risk management-related matters; (ii) overseeing and assessing any ESG-related risks that we may
face in our business operations; (iii) fostering a corporate culture of safety and strictly implementing
the occupational health and safety system to ensure that all health and safety factors are taken into
account; (iv) identifying and assessing climate-related risks and opportunities that have potential
impacts on us; (v) developing strategies of responding to climate change, setting targets of reducing
greenhouse gas (“GHG”) emissions and guiding implementation efforts; (vi) conducting regular
discussions to discuss and determine ESG-related issues required to be addressed; (vii) reporting to
our Board on ESG-related risks and opportunities; and (viii) advising our Board on ESG reports,
strategies, initiatives and objectives. We will also engage with independent third-party advisers as our
ESG adviser (“ESGAdvisers”) to assess our ESG-related risks and provide professional advice to our
Board when necessary.
We integrate our business development, industry characteristics and national policies with the
expectations of stakeholders in identification, assessment and selection of material ESG-related
topics. Through stakeholder surveys and industry analysis, we determine our material issues and focus
on addressing them during our business development process. The most important ESG-related topics
we have identified include adaptation to climate change, environmental compliance, ecological
protection, labour management, occupational health and safety, business ethics and anti-corruption.
Identification and Assessment of ESG-related Risks
Based on the aforesaid ESG topics, we systematically assess ESG risks related to our operations.
Our ESG risks mainly involve (i) environmental risks, including physical and transition risks from the
climate change, risk of environmental violations due to non-compliant disposal of pollutants and
ecological damage risks from mining operations, and other natural disaster risks including but not
limited to earthquakes; (ii) social risks, such as health and safety hazards for employees during our
business operations and (iii) governance risks, such as corruption risks resulting from non-compliance
incidents conducted by employees and suppliers, leading to damage to our interests and brand image.
We strictly adopt occupational health and safety production measures in accordance with regulatory
requirements during our business operations. Moreover, we organise safety inspections on a monthly
basis and promptly rectify any issues discovered to effectively safeguard the occupational health and
safety of our employees. To further understand the impact of these risks on our ESG development, we
set out the risk content and employ quantifiable risk indicators for further detection and control,

Identification, Assessment and Management of Climate-related Risks and Opportunities
Climate change is a major global challenge and one of the key factors that may affect our
sustainability. To minimise its impact, we pay attention to climate governance, seek measures for
managing climate change impact and make climate action a pillar of our ESG efforts. Based on the
recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosure (“TCFD”), we have
initially identified climate-related risks and opportunities considering our business characteristics,
and expect to regularly monitor, assess and analyse such risks. In response to the climate-related risks
and opportunities identified, we have also prepared countermeasures and initiatives for our
operations. Furthermore, we plan to regularly monitor climate-related risks and take on our corporate
environmental responsibility to mitigate the adverse impacts of climate change.

Climate-related opportunities
In addition to the aforementioned the physical and transition risks, we recognise that climate
change may likewise present us from seizing business opportunities. In particular, we have identified
the following opportunities, which will allow us to extend operating time in winter, improve resource
efficiency, use more low-carbon energy to reduce operational emissions, facilitate the low-carbon
transition and promote sustainable business operation:
• Operating time may increase as fewer snowstorms due to the rising temperature, which
increases the amount of production and helps to generate more revenue for our Group;

Environmental Protection
We believe that the prevalent global trend in sustainability is focused on “going green” and
transitioning to low-carbon energy. As we are committed to environmental responsibility, we have
implemented a range of measures to enhance our eco-friendliness and pursue high-quality and
sustainable development.
Environmental compliance
We should comply with a number of environmental laws and regulations including the
Environmental Protection Law of the PRC 《( 中華人民共和國環境保護法》), the Water Pollution
Prevention and Control Law of the PRC 《( 中華人民共和國水污染防治法》) and the Regulation of
Xizang Autonomous Region on Environmental Protection 《( 西藏自治區環境保護條例》), to name a
few. Therefore, we self-regulate our environmental protection practices and conduct environmental
impact assessments in accordance with these laws and regulations. During the Track Record Period,
we did not receive any notice or warning with respect to environment protection , nor were we subject
to any material fine or penalty that had a material adverse effect on our operations.
Going forward, we will continue to improve our internal management policies on environmental
protection and green production, taking into account the requirements of local environmental
protection authorities, established good practices and the progress and condition of our operation. We
will also enhance the management and control of wastewater, dust waste, by strengthening inspections
and monitoring. Compliance costs are expected to rise as we continue to expand our business,
nonetheless, such costs are expected to a relatively small portion of our overall operating cost and will
not have a significant impact on our financial performance.
Environmental management
Environmental management is of high priority on our ESG agenda, and we have the Safety and
Environment Department to enhance our environment management. We have integrated the principles
of green production into our operations to reduce adverse impacts of our operations on the
environment. In particular, we focus on managing wastewater, dust, solid waste and hazardous waste
from our operation to ensure compliance with relevant disposal requirements. We have developed a
robust environmental management system aligned with standards and we have obtained ISO
14001:2015 certification. This system has explicitly defined responsibilities for both environmental
and business matters, enabling us to continuously improve our environmental performance and
achieve sustainable production.

BUSINESS
We endeavour to promote green operations, save energy and lower consumption in the
operational sites and office, improve resource utilisation and raise environmental awareness among
the workforces. We also aim to optimise financial performance by strengthening runtime management,
reducing downtime, improving equipment efficiency, benchmarking against best practices and
lowering unit consumption. Our specific energy conservation measures include but are not limited to
(i) replacing old transformers with energy-saving electric transformers to reduce the active and
reactive power loss of equipment; (ii) using energy-efficient LED light sources and lamps for lighting.
In addition, we have formulated guidelines to control and supervise the usage of vehicles owned
by us. Specific measures include (i) regulating the use of vehicles, going through the
insurance-related procedures in accordance with the vehicle management regulations of the PRC,
carrying out regular maintenance checks and oil usage inspections, controlling expenditures and
cutting down expenses; and (ii) prohibition on use of a vehicle without permission and requiring
detailed record for each use (including the approver, mileage, driver and other relevant details).
Dust control: During the mining operations, the main sources of dust are usage of our owned
vehicles and machinery. We have set up hydraulic sprays and dust collecting machines to control dust
during our operations. In addition, we perform systematic, preventive inspections on a regular basis
to reduce the emission of exhaust pollutants. During production equipment inspections, we will also
take the following measures to reduce air pollutant emissions: (i) ensuring that environmental
parameters (such as dust, noise and vibration of machines, equipment and transport facilities) during
the runtime can meet the required standards by the Government; and (ii) using high-quality diesel fuel
to fuel machinery and vehicles and minimise engine idling.
Wastewater management: the wastewater generated from our construction and operations mainly
include production wastewater and domestic sewage. The production wastewater generated from the
processing plant will be collected and transported by a submersible sewage pump to the return tank
in the tailings pond for further collection and reuse. We have implemented a fully enclosed water
recycling system with no discharge, and the production water reuse rate in the processing plant has
achieved approximately 86.8%. Domestic sewage will also be discharged after treatment and then
used for fertilising grassland.
Waste management: our wastes primarily include, tailings and domestic waste. After ore
processing from the processing plant, tailings produced will all be pumped to the tailings pond for
storage and disposal. In addition, domestic waste will be collected after classification, and transported
and processed by third parties. Furthermore, we have formulated detailed guidelines on the treatment
of hazardous waste. Hazardous waste is collected and then entrusted to qualified units for disposal.
We have also contracted with a qualified third-party waste disposal company for the disposal of
hazardous waste. We are required to promptly report on the occurrence of any loss, leakage or
diffusion of hazardous waste to the relevant health authorities and to keep proper records of such
accidents.

As advised by our PRC Legal Advisers, mining companies in the PRC are required to prepare

approval by the relevant authorities. In addition, mining companies must establish a dedicated mine

COMPETITION
Summary
The competitive landscape for zinc, lead and copper concentrates in China is characterised by
a combination of domestic production dynamics, global supply chain challenges and fluctuating
demand. The future development for the zinc, lead and copper concentrates will depend on the market
players’ ability to address these challenges while capitalising on emerging opportunities.
− 232 −

=== PAGE 243 ===
BUSINESS
Zinc Concentrates
The global supply market for zinc concentrates has experienced a declining trend, with a CAGR
of approximately -1.2% from 2018 to 2024. However, from 2025 to 2028, the global zinc concentrate
supply is expected to recover, with a projected CAGR of 1.8% driven by new mining projects. Despite
being the largest consumer and producer of zinc concentrates, China has experienced fluctuations in
domestic production. Following a decline from 2018 to 2020, production of zinc concentrates surged
in 2021. Going forward, both domestic production and imports are projected to rise from 2025 to
2028, supporting overall demand for zinc concentrates. In Xizang, the annual zinc concentrate
production was approximately 111.3 kt in 2024, with the market still dominated by small-scale
producers.
Lead Concentrates
China stands as the world’s largest producer of lead concentrates, contributing over 33.0% to the
global supply. Going forward, China’s lead concentrate production is projected to grow at a CAGR
of approximately 2.0% from 2025 to 2028. While global demand is expected to decrease slightly from
2018 to 2024, a rebound is anticipated from 2025 to 2028, reflecting an increase in end-use
consumption of lead concentrates. In Xizang, the annual lead concentrate production was
approximately 88.2 kt in 2024, with a competitive landscape dominated by a few key producers.
Copper Concentrates
The copper concentrate market exhibits a more concentrated supply compared to lead and zinc
concentrates. From 2018 to 2024, global copper concentrate production grew at a CAGR of
approximately 1.9%, bolstered by the commissioning of new projects in the mining industry. This
upward trend is expected to continue, with anticipated for the period from 2025 to 2028. China’s
copper concentrate production has also demonstrated steady growth, increasing from 1,532.0 kt to
1,982.0 kt between 2018 and 2024, with a CAGR of approximately 4.4%. In Xizang, the annual copper
concentrate production was approximately 376.4 kt in 2024, characterised by a competitive landscape
with a few dominant producers.
To the best knowledge of our Directors, during the Track Record Period, we did not have any
overlapping of customer base with our customers which are nonferrous metal traders. As disclosed
above, our customers include traders which are the trading arms of group companies engaged in
refinery business but do not include downstream refineries which refine concentrates into metal
ingots. See “Business — Our Customers — Overview” in this prospectus for details. Therefore, there
is no material overlap of customers of the Group and their downstream customers. The risk of
potential competition between the Group and the nonferrous metal trader customers is remote. The
delineation between our customer base and the customer base of our customers helps reduce the risk
of potential conflicts of interest between us and our customers such as preferential pricing or contract
terms. The delineation also serves to support fair and independent commercial relationships, which
contributes to the stability of our supply chain and sales channels.
